03 THE DAILY RITUAL

NINE STEPS / TWO HOURS / EVERY CARD, EVERY DAY
01
REVIEW
15 min · old material, from memory
02
CONCEPT
what & why engineers use it
03
ALTERNATIVES
and when to pick each
04
ROADBLOCK → FIX
the wall everyone hits, and the fix
05
READ
two sources · with the concept, a 20-min learn block
06
BUILD & SAVE
55 min · the real test, git commit = checkpoint
07
PRACTICE
15 min · one timed SQL or algorithm rep
08
DONE WHEN
the cutoff checklist
09
RECALL
15 min · boss check, book closed

The order is the point. You read only after you know why the thing exists, you build only after you know what breaks, and the day does not close until you can say it back with the book shut. The day opens with a review because pulling old material out of memory, a little later each time, is what makes it last. A day is cleared when its tests pass and the commit lands — not when you have read it.

EVERY LINK FROM THE PLAN / GROUPED BY HOW YOU USE IT
01 Courses that back the plan +

  • LLM Zoomcamp (free) — github.com/DataTalksClub/llm-zoomcamp — RAG, hybrid search, evaluation, monitoring. Use for: Days 50–56.
  • DeepLearning.AI short courses — deeplearning.ai/short-courses — take the short ones as add-ons: Pydantic for LLM Workflows (Day 47), MCP (Day 58), guardrails (Day 60), RAG (Days 50–52), agentic AI (Days 57–58), orchestrating workflows for GenAI (Day 31).

02 Memory tools — spaced repetition +
  • error-log.md — your own file. Every miss, with the date and a one-line correction. Review the last 14 days every week and before any real interview.
  • Anki — apps.ankiweb.net — free flashcards with built-in spacing. Use for: cloud service maps (Day 33), definitions (Days 43–49), SCD and isolation tables.
  • Paper Leitner box — five piles reviewed on days 1, 3, 7, 14 and 30. The same schedule as the card reviews, with no software.

01 Python Syntax — muscle-memory templates +

Loops & Iteration

for i, item in enumerate(items): ... # with index
for a, b in zip(list_a, list_b): ... # parallel
for key, value in d.items(): ... # dict pairs
for item in reversed(items): ... # reverse
for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1): ... # n-1 down to 0

Comprehensions

[x * 2 for x in nums if x > 0] # filter + map
{x: x * 2 for x in nums} # dict comp
{x for x in nums} # set comp

Dict / Set / Counter

d.get(key, 0); d.setdefault(key, [])
from collections import Counter, defaultdict, deque
Counter(items).most_common(k) # top-k
d = defaultdict(list); d["k"].append(x)
d = defaultdict(int); d["k"] += 1

Sorting

sorted(items, key=lambda x: (-x.score, x.name)) # multi-key, desc primary
items.sort() # in-place

Heap

import heapq
heapq.heappush(heap, (priority, item))
heapq.heappop(heap) # smallest first
heapq.nlargest(k, items); heapq.nsmallest(k, items)
# Max-heap: negate priorities

Strings

s.lower(); s.upper(); s.strip(); s.split(); ",".join(words)
s.isalnum(); s.isalpha(); s.isdigit()
ord('A') # 65; chr(65) # 'A'; s[::-1] # reverse

Production Python

 db_url: str
 retry_max: int = 3

def fragile_call(): ...

 return await asyncio.gather(*(fetch(u) for u in urls))
02 SQL Patterns — windows, sessions, MERGE, SCD2, plans +

Window functions

ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC, id) -- exactly N rows
RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) -- ties share a rank, then a gap
DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) -- ties share, no gap
SUM(x) OVER (PARTITION BY u ORDER BY ts ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
AVG(x) OVER (ORDER BY d ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) -- 7-row moving average
LAG(x) OVER (PARTITION BY u ORDER BY ts, id) -- always a unique ORDER BY

Default-frame trap: with an ORDER BY and no frame, SUM() OVER uses RANGE, so ties share a running total. Write ROWS.

Top-N per group, and dedup (latest row per key)

WITH ranked AS (
 SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY k ORDER BY updated_at DESC, id DESC) rn FROM t
) SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1; -- rn <= 3 for top 3; QUALIFY rn = 1 where supported

Sessions (30-minute timeout)

WITH f AS (
 SELECT *, CASE WHEN LAG(ts) OVER w IS NULL
 OR ts - LAG(ts) OVER w > INTERVAL '30 minutes' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS new_s
 FROM events WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY u ORDER BY ts, id))
SELECT *, SUM(new_s) OVER (PARTITION BY u ORDER BY ts, id) AS session_id FROM f;

Gaps and islands: date − ROW_NUMBER() is constant inside an unbroken run, so group by it.

SELECT u, MIN(d) AS start_d, MAX(d) AS end_d, COUNT(*) AS days
FROM (SELECT u, d, d - (ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY u ORDER BY d))::int AS grp
 FROM (SELECT DISTINCT u, d FROM activity) a) t
GROUP BY u, grp;

Idempotent upsert (MERGE; syntax varies by engine)

MERGE INTO target t USING (latest-per-key of the batch) s ON t.id = s.id
WHEN MATCHED AND s.op = 'D' THEN DELETE
WHEN MATCHED AND s.updated_at > t.updated_at THEN UPDATE SET ...
WHEN NOT MATCHED AND s.op <> 'D' THEN INSERT ...;

SCD type 2: valid_to = COALESCE(LEAD(valid_from) OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY valid_from), '9999-12-31'); one is_current row per key; point-in-time join ON f.cust = d.cust AND f.ts >= d.valid_from AND f.ts < d.valid_to.

Joins: INNER (matches only) · LEFT (all left + NULLs) · FULL OUTER · CROSS (date-spine fills) · Anti-join NOT EXISTS or LEFT JOIN … WHERE r.id IS NULL. NOT IN returns nothing if the list holds a NULL. A filter on the right table of a LEFT JOIN belongs in ON.

Fan-out: joining to the many side multiplies the one side's measures. Aggregate first, or sum at the measure's own grain.

Recursive CTE (hierarchy)

WITH RECURSIVE hierarchy AS (
 SELECT id, manager_id, 1 AS depth FROM employees WHERE id = ?
 UNION ALL
 SELECT e.id, e.manager_id, h.depth + 1 FROM employees e JOIN hierarchy h ON e.id = h.manager_id
) SELECT * FROM hierarchy;

Plan operators: Nested Loop (small outer + indexed inner) · Hash Join (large, no index) · Merge Join (both sorted on key) · Index Seek (good) vs Scan (bad unless tiny). Compare estimated vs actual rows.

Isolation: READ UNCOMMITTED (dirty) · READ COMMITTED (default) · REPEATABLE READ · SNAPSHOT (readers do not block writers) · SERIALIZABLE (stops write skew).

Indexing: narrow, ever-increasing clustered keys; covering indexes with included columns; WHERE and JOIN columns first; filtered indexes for skewed predicates.

CDC: log-based capture gives inserts, updates and deletes with an op type and a sequence number. Apply the latest change per key by sequence; a delete is a tombstone; replays must be idempotent.

03 Data Modeling — grain, stars, SCDs +

Four steps: business process → grain (one sentence: "one row per order line") → dimensions → facts. Say the grain before anything else.

Fact types: additive (revenue: sum across anything) · semi-additive (balance: not across time) · non-additive (ratio: store numerator and denominator).

Dimensions: surrogate keys; conformed dimensions shared across facts; a date dimension every time; degenerate dimension (the order number lives on the fact); junk dimension for low-cardinality flags.

Star vs snowflake vs one big table: star is the default; snowflake saves space at the cost of joins; one big table is fast for BI and hard to keep consistent.

Kimball vs Inmon vs Data Vault: Kimball = conformed dimensions, bottom-up marts · Inmon = normalized enterprise warehouse first · Data Vault = hubs, links, satellites for auditability.

SCD: Type 1 overwrite · Type 2 new row with validity dates · Type 3 previous-value column · Type 6 hybrid. Pick 2 when the business asks "as it was then".

Mid-round change checklist: does the grain change? does a dimension need history? does a measure now sit at a different grain? re-state, then adjust.

Mixed-grain trap: order-level shipping on order-line rows multiplies in a SUM. Keep each measure at its own grain.

Reconcile: fact totals must equal the source totals; test it.

05 HLD Concepts +

Scale axes: throughput (RPS) · latency (p50/p99/p999) · storage (GB/day) · durability (RPO) & availability (RTO, SLO 9s) · consistency model.

Consistency: CAP (under partition choose C or A); PACELC (else: latency vs consistency). Linearizable > sequential > causal > eventual. SI allows write-skew; serializable doesn't.

Replication: leader-follower (sync = strong/lower-availability, async = stale reads) · leaderless quorum (R+W>N) · multi-leader (conflicts → CRDT/LWW).

Partitioning: hash (even, no range) · range (scans, hot ranges) · composite · consistent hashing (minimal movement on resize) · hot-partition fix = salt the key.

Caching: cache-aside (most common) · write-through · write-back · eviction LRU/LFU/TTL · stampede → locks/coalescing/early expiration.

Streaming: at-most-once / at-least-once (needs idempotency) / exactly-once (idempotency keys + tx + dedup) · backpressure = bounded queue or pull-based.

Reliability: idempotency keys · transactional outbox · circuit breaker (closed→open→half-open) · bulkhead · DLQ + replay · saga.

DDIA map: Ch5 Replication · Ch6 Partitioning · Ch7 Transactions · Ch8 Trouble · Ch9 Consensus · Ch11 Stream processing.

06 LLD Concepts +

SOLID: SRP (one reason to change) · Open/closed · Liskov · Interface-segregation · Dependency-inversion (inject abstractions).

Patterns: Strategy (swappable algorithm, such as a scoring model) · Factory · Builder · Observer (pub/sub = Kafka) · Decorator (@retry, @cache) · Adapter · Chain of Responsibility · Repository · Unit of Work.

OOD template: clarify scope → nouns=classes → verbs=methods → relationships (composition vs inheritance) → interfaces first → walk one flow → extension points.

Python OOD: Protocol over ABC · @dataclass(frozen=True) for value objects · __slots__ for memory · composition over inheritance.

07 Interview Frameworks +

Coding talk-track (9 steps): restate → clarify edges → brute force + complexity → name bottleneck + the change → confirm → code while narrating → trace example → edge cases → scale follow-up.

System design (Hello Interview, ~7 min/phase): requirements (functional + non-functional) → core entities → API → high-level design → deep dives (where you earn the offer) → tradeoffs.

STAR: Situation 15s · Task 10s · Action 45s · Result-with-metric 20s.

Save phrases when stuck: "let me think out loud about why this is hard" · "can I try a small example by hand" · "brute force first, then optimize" · "there's a tradeoff here — let me name both options."

08 LLM, RAG and Evals — the one-page sheet +

Tokens and context: the model reads tokens; cost = input × price + output × price; the context window holds prompt + answer. Details in the middle of long prompts are recalled less reliably.

Sampling: temperature reshapes the distribution; top-p keeps the smallest set of tokens adding to p; top-k keeps the k best. Temperature 0 is near-deterministic, not guaranteed.

Attention: softmax(Q·Kᵀ / √d) · V. √d keeps scores from saturating the softmax; the causal mask hides the future. Cost grows with the square of context length. KV cache stores past keys and values. Prefill is parallel, decode is sequential.

Encoder vs decoder vs both: encoder = embeddings, classification · decoder = generation, chat, tools · encoder-decoder = translation, summarization.

Which lever: facts that change → RAG · behaviour or format → prompt, then fine-tune · cost or latency → smaller model, quantization, caching.

Adapters and training: LoRA trains small low-rank adapters · QLoRA does it on a 4-bit base · quantization = fewer bits per weight (cheaper serving, some quality loss) · RLHF = supervised tune → reward model from preferences → policy optimization (DPO skips the reward model).

ML metrics: precision = flagged and right ÷ flagged · recall = found ÷ existing · PR-AUC for rare positives · accuracy lies on imbalanced data · split by time · fit scalers on the training split only.

RAG stages and where it fails: ingest → chunk → embed → retrieve (hybrid) → rerank → assemble prompt → generate → cite. Debug in that order; the first failing stage is the cause.

Retrieval metrics: recall@k · MRR = mean of 1/rank of the first hit · NDCG = rank-discounted gain. Generation metrics: faithfulness, answer relevancy, context precision, context recall.

LLM judge: label a sample yourself, measure agreement, fix the rubric, re-check after any change. Known biases: length, self-preference.

API contract: schema (Pydantic) · structured output or tool call · validate · one repair retry · timeout · bounded retries · versioned prompt · log tokens, latency, cost.

Agent vs workflow: if you can draw the steps, it is a workflow. Agents need tool schemas, an allow-list, and budgets (steps, tokens, dollars, seconds).

Security: treat retrieved text as data; allow-list tools; filter permissions inside the retrieval query; cap cost; return a safe fallback.

Cost and latency: measure p50 and p95 per stage · prompt cache (static prefix first) · scoped semantic cache · route easy requests to a small model · fewer, tighter chunks.

07 PLAYGROUND

PYTHON AND SQL / FREE / RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER / NO SIGN-IN, NO SERVER
CTRL / ⌘ + ENTER RUNS / ESC THEN TAB LEAVES THE EDITOR
HOW IT WORKS, AND WHAT IT CANNOT DO
  • Python is CPython compiled to WebAssembly (Pyodide). It starts the first time you press RUN, in a background worker, so RESET PYTHON or STOP ends a runaway loop without freezing the page. Variables stay between runs until you reset. Top-level await works.
  • Packages: the standard library, pydantic, pytest, numpy, pandas, sqlite3 and most other popular libraries load by name when you import them. For a pure-Python package from PyPI, put # pip: name on the first line.
  • SQL is DuckDB, also compiled to WebAssembly. It matches the DuckDB used in the sql-lab repo, so QUALIFY, window frames, generate_series and EXPLAIN ANALYZE work. LOAD SAMPLE WAREHOUSE builds five small tables with planted problems: duplicates, NULLs and orphan keys. The data lives in memory and is gone when you reload.
  • Not here: requests and urllib calls (a browser has no raw sockets), input(), threads, subprocesses, your local files, Spark, Airflow and dbt. Do the real build in your repo; use this to try an idea in one minute.
  • Download: each runtime is roughly 10 MB the first time, from a public CDN (jsDelivr), then your browser caches it. Your code stays in this browser only.
  • Try it from a card: every Python and SQL code block in the day cards and cheat sheets has a TRY IN PLAYGROUND button that copies it into the editor.

three dedup queries return identical rows, and you can say what a NULL does to NOT IN, COUNT(col) and a LEFT JOIN filter.
01REVIEW

Cold start. You have not studied this yet, so a wrong answer is fine. Write your best answer to each in two or three lines. You re-test these on Day 7.

02CONCEPT

Interviewers start with joins and dedup because they expose whether you think about grain: what one row of each table means. A join that multiplies rows (a fan-out) silently breaks every SUM after it. Dedup means keeping one row per key by a rule you can defend, usually "latest by updated_at": ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY key ORDER BY updated_at DESC) = 1.

03ALTERNATIVES
  • ROW_NUMBER filter — the default. Add a tie-breaker so the result is deterministic.
  • QUALIFY (DuckDB, Snowflake, BigQuery) or DISTINCT ON (Postgres) — shorter, not portable to SQL Server or MySQL.
  • GROUP BY + MAX, then join back — works everywhere, but ties return duplicate rows.
  • NOT EXISTS vs LEFT JOIN … IS NULL vs NOT IN — NOT EXISTS and the anti-join are safe; NOT IN returns nothing if the subquery contains a NULL.
04ROADBLOCK → FIX

Fan-out: join orders to order_items, then SUM(orders.amount) — every order is counted once per item. Fix: aggregate the many side first, or sum at the grain the measure lives at. Second wall: a filter on the right table in WHERE turns a LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN. Put it in ON.

05KEY IDEAS / HINTS
  • Say the grain before you join: "one row per order".
  • COUNT(col) skips NULLs, COUNT(*) does not, and = NULL is never true — use IS NULL.
  • Inside ROW_NUMBER, always end the ORDER BY with a unique column.
06READ
  • PostgreSQL tutorial — Joins Between Tables — extract: inner vs outer, and what the NULL side looks like.
  • Mode — SQL joins — extract: where a filter belongs in an outer join.

02 ○ UPCOMING

Window functions I: ranking, top-N, running totals

0 / 170 XP
CUTOFF TARGET
top-N per group in three tie rules, a running total with an explicit frame, and a 7-day moving average over a date spine — each tested on sql-lab.
01REVIEW

Answer each aloud or on paper before you look anything up. A miss goes into error-log.md with one line of correction.

02CONCEPT

A window function computes a value for each row from a set of related rows without collapsing them the way GROUP BY does. It has three parts: PARTITION BY (the groups), ORDER BY (the order inside a group) and a frame (which neighbouring rows count). Ranking has three flavours: ROW_NUMBER (never ties), RANK (ties share a rank, then a gap) and DENSE_RANK (ties share, no gap). The classic question is "top 3 per group", then the interviewer changes the tie rule.

03ALTERNATIVES
  • ROW_NUMBER / RANK / DENSE_RANK — pick by the tie rule: exactly N rows, everyone tied at rank N, or N distinct values.
  • Window vs correlated subquery vs self-join — a window is one pass and the easiest to read; self-joins fan out.
  • ROWS vs RANGE frame — ROWS counts physical rows; RANGE includes every row with the same ORDER BY value.
  • CTE filter vs QUALIFY — window results cannot go in WHERE; wrap in a CTE for portability.
04ROADBLOCK → FIX

The default frame trap: SUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY ts) uses RANGE … CURRENT ROW, so two rows with the same ts get the same running total. Fix: write the frame (ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) or add a unique tie-breaker. Second wall: a moving average over missing days is wrong. Build a date spine first and LEFT JOIN to it.

05KEY IDEAS / HINTS
  • Window functions run after WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING, and before the final ORDER BY and LIMIT.
  • An empty OVER () means one partition: the whole table.
  • 7-day average: AVG(x) OVER (ORDER BY d ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), one row per day.
06READ
  • PostgreSQL tutorial — Window Functions — extract: partition, order and what the frame is.
  • Mode — SQL window functions — extract: ranking and running totals side by side.

Window functions II: LAG/LEAD, sessions, gaps and islands

0 / 170 XP
CUTOFF TARGET
sessionize an event stream with LAG, find consecutive-day streaks with the row-number trick, and say why ORDER BY inside the window is not optional.
01REVIEW

Answer each aloud or on paper before you look anything up. A miss goes into error-log.md with one line of correction.

02CONCEPT

LAG and LEAD read the previous or next row in the window order. Most "compare to the row before" questions use them: day-over-day change, time between events, a new session when the gap passes 30 minutes. Gaps and islands groups consecutive rows: subtract a row number from a date and every row in an unbroken run gets the same value.

03ALTERNATIVES
  • LAG/LEAD vs self-join on id+1 — the self-join breaks when ids have holes; LAG follows the ORDER BY.
  • date − ROW_NUMBER() vs LAG flag + running SUM — the subtraction trick only fits exact-step runs; the flag version handles timeouts (sessions).
  • SQL vs pandas/Polars — SQL when the data is big and already in the warehouse; Python when the logic needs custom state.
04ROADBLOCK → FIX

LAG with no ORDER BY, or an order on a non-unique column, gives neighbours that change between runs. It "works" on your laptop and fails in production. Fix: order by a unique key such as (ts, event_id). Second wall: the first row has no previous row, so LAG is NULL — decide what NULL means (usually "new session") and handle it.

05KEY IDEAS / HINTS
  • Session id = SUM(is_new_session) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts), where is_new_session is ts − LAG(ts) > 30 minutes OR LAG(ts) IS NULL.
  • Islands: d − ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY d) is constant inside a run of consecutive days.
  • Longest streak per user = the biggest island.
06READ
  • PostgreSQL — window function reference — extract: lag, lead and their default-value argument.
  • Mode — SQL window functions — extract: the LAG/LEAD section.

04 ○ UPCOMING

Idempotent MERGE, late data and incremental loads

0 / 170 XP
CUTOFF TARGET
a MERGE-based upsert you can run twice with the same result, and a late-arriving row that corrects history without double counting.
01REVIEW

Answer each aloud or on paper before you look anything up. A miss goes into error-log.md with one line of correction.

02CONCEPT

Pipelines re-run: retries, backfills, replays. An idempotent load leaves the table in the same state no matter how many times you apply the same batch. In SQL that means an upsert by business key (MERGE, or INSERT … ON CONFLICT) with a rule for which version wins — not a blind INSERT. Late data arrives after its window closed; you either reload a lookback window or let the upsert correct the row.

03ALTERNATIVES
  • MERGE vs INSERT … ON CONFLICT vs delete-and-insert by partition — MERGE handles insert, update and delete in one statement; ON CONFLICT needs a unique constraint; delete-and-insert by partition is the simplest idempotent load for append-only facts.
  • Full refresh vs high-water-mark incremental vs CDC log — full refresh is safest for small tables; a watermark needs a trustworthy timestamp; only CDC sees deletes.
  • Exact watermark vs lookback window — a lookback (reload the last 3 days) absorbs late data at the cost of rework.
04ROADBLOCK → FIX

Duplicate keys inside one batch make MERGE fail ("multiple source rows match") or apply in random order. Fix: dedup the batch first (Day 1), then MERGE. Second wall: a replayed old batch overwrites newer data. Fix: guard the update with WHEN MATCHED AND src.updated_at > tgt.updated_at.

05KEY IDEAS / HINTS
  • Idempotent means apply(apply(x)) == apply(x).
  • The MERGE ON clause is the business key, never a surrogate you generate.
  • MERGE never removes rows by itself — deletes need a tombstone flag or an explicit WHEN MATCHED AND src.op = 'D' THEN DELETE.
06READ
  • PostgreSQL — MERGE — extract: WHEN MATCHED / NOT MATCHED and the extra AND conditions.
  • Delta Lake — upsert with MERGE — extract: the same pattern at lakehouse scale; you meet it again on Day 24.

05 ○ UPCOMING

Dimensional modeling: declare the grain first

0 / 170 XP
CUTOFF TARGET
a star schema for orders (fact, customer, product and date dimensions) with the grain written in one sentence, answering three business questions.
01REVIEW

Answer each aloud or on paper before you look anything up. A miss goes into error-log.md with one line of correction.

02CONCEPT

Dimensional modeling splits data into facts (events you measure: an order line, a click) and dimensions (the context: customer, product, date). The habit interviewers reward is declaring the grain first — "one row per order line" — and only then choosing the dimensions and measures that are true at that grain. Measures can be additive (revenue), semi-additive (a balance: not summable across time) or non-additive (a ratio: store numerator and denominator). Surrogate keys decouple the warehouse from source ids and make history possible.

03ALTERNATIVES
  • Star vs snowflake vs one big table — star is the default (simple joins); snowflake normalizes dimensions (less space, more joins); one big table is fast for BI but hard to keep consistent.
  • Kimball vs Inmon vs Data Vault — Kimball builds conformed dimensions and marts bottom-up; Inmon builds a normalized enterprise warehouse first; Data Vault (hubs, links, satellites) favors auditability. Default to Kimball unless the prompt says otherwise.
  • Surrogate vs natural keys — surrogate keys survive source-system changes and enable SCD2.
04ROADBLOCK → FIX

Mixed grain: order-level shipping cost copied onto every order-line row, then SUM(shipping) multiplies it. Fix: keep each measure at its own grain — an order-grain fact, or an explicit allocation. Second wall: modeling the source tables instead of the business process. Start from "what is being measured", not from the schema you were handed.

05KEY IDEAS / HINTS
  • Four steps: business process → grain → dimensions → facts.
  • A degenerate dimension (the order number) lives on the fact with no table of its own.
  • A date dimension is worth building every time; a junk dimension collects low-cardinality flags.
06READ

  • Microsoft Learn — star schema guidance — extract: fact vs dimension tables and why the shape helps reporting.

06 ○ UPCOMING

SCD types and reading a query plan

0 / 170 XP
CUTOFF TARGET
dim_customer as SCD type 2, a point-in-time join that returns the version valid at order time, and an EXPLAIN you can read aloud.
01REVIEW

Answer each aloud or on paper before you look anything up. A miss goes into error-log.md with one line of correction.

02CONCEPT

A slowly changing dimension is a dimension whose attributes change over time (a customer moves region). Type 1 overwrites (no history). Type 2 closes the old row and inserts a new one with validity dates (full history). Type 3 keeps the previous value in an extra column (one step of history). Interviewers ask which you would pick, then change the requirement mid-round: "finance now wants last year's revenue by the region the customer lived in then." A query plan (EXPLAIN) shows how the engine runs your SQL — scan, filter, join type, sort, aggregate. You are looking for full scans, a bad join order, and row estimates far from reality.

03ALTERNATIVES
  • Type 1 vs 2 vs 3 vs 6 — 1 when history is worthless, 2 when the business asks "as it was then", 3 for a single before/after column, 6 is a hybrid you only name.
  • SCD2 via MERGE vs a snapshot tool (dbt snapshots) — know both; you meet dbt on Day 29.
  • Join by date range at query time vs store the dimension key on the fact at load time — resolving the key once at load is cheaper and safer.
04ROADBLOCK → FIX

Overlapping or gapped validity ranges after a late-arriving change. Fix: derive valid_to from LEAD(valid_from) so ranges are contiguous by construction, use 9999-12-31 rather than NULL for the open row, and test for overlaps. Second wall: reading a plan by cost number alone. Compare estimated rows with actual rows and look at what is scanned.

05KEY IDEAS / HINTS
  • Make valid_to exclusive: valid_from <= ts AND ts < valid_to.
  • One is_current row per business key — write a test for it.
  • In a plan: which scan, which join (hash, merge, nested loop), where the filter is applied, estimated vs actual rows.
06READ
  • Kimball Group — Type 2 slowly changing dimension — extract: the row-versioning mechanics.
  • PostgreSQL — Using EXPLAIN — extract: how to read nodes, costs and actual rows.

08 ○ UPCOMING

Types, Pydantic and fail-loud settings

0 / 170 XP
CUTOFF TARGET
mypy --strict passes on sentinel/models.py, and Sentinel-Lite refuses to start on a bad config: it fails at startup, not mid-run.
01REVIEW

Answer each aloud or on paper before you look anything up. A miss goes into error-log.md with one line of correction.

02CONCEPT

Type hints plus a checker such as mypy catch shape bugs before the code runs. They do nothing at runtime, so data from outside (files, APIs, environment variables) still needs validation. That is Pydantic's job: it parses untrusted input into typed objects and raises a precise error when the input is wrong. Settings follow the same rule: load config once, validate it at startup, and refuse to run on bad values. Today you build the typed core of Sentinel-Lite.

03ALTERNATIVES
  • Pydantic — runtime validation at I/O boundaries (the default choice today). Pick when data is untrusted.
  • dataclasses (Day 9) — internal value objects you already trust; no validation overhead.
  • TypedDict — static-only hints for dict-shaped data; zero runtime cost, zero runtime safety.
  • attrs / marshmallow — older ecosystems; Pydantic v2 (Rust core) is faster and now the default for new work.
04ROADBLOCK → FIX

The classic wall: mypy --strict floods you with error: Function is missing a type annotation and Need type annotation for.... Beginners disable strict; engineers instead annotate incrementally and use reveal_type(x) to see what mypy infers, plus # type: ignore[code] sparingly on genuinely untypeable third-party calls. The fix is precision, not surrender.

The big one migrating to v2: validators changed. People hit @validator is deprecated and confusing ValidationErrors. The fix the community reaches for: use @field_validator (v2 name) and model_config = ConfigDict(...) instead of the old class Config, and read the error's .errors() list — it tells you exactly which field and rule failed. Second gotcha: Pydantic coerces ("5" → 5) which can hide bugs; use Strict types when you want hard rejection.

05KEY IDEAS / HINTS
  • BaseSettings auto-loads from env vars / .env.
  • Fail-fast: validate everything you depend on before doing real work.
  • TypedDict vs Pydantic = static-only hint vs runtime-enforced. Use both, in their lanes (internal vs boundary).
06READ

  • Pydantic v2 — Models — extract: validation/coercion + field_validator.

09 ○ UPCOMING

Value objects, Protocols and SOLID in practice

0 / 170 XP
CUTOFF TARGET
Mismatch and RemediationReport are frozen, slotted dataclasses, and a third detector plugs into the orchestrator with zero orchestrator edits.
01REVIEW

Answer each aloud or on paper before you look anything up. A miss goes into error-log.md with one line of correction.

02CONCEPT

Internal objects you already trust do not need Pydantic. A @dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True) is a cheap, immutable value object, and slots drops the per-instance __dict__, which saves memory when you hold millions of them. Design the moving parts around interfaces: a Protocol describes what an object can do, so the orchestrator depends on Detector and Remediator, not on concrete classes. Pass collaborators in through the constructor (dependency injection) instead of subclassing to share code.

03ALTERNATIVES
  • Protocol — structural interface, no inheritance required. Default in modern Python.
  • ABC (abstractmethod) — nominal interface; pick when you want to share base implementation or force explicit subclassing.
  • Duck typing, no interface — fine for tiny scripts; doesn't scale to a team or a checker.
04ROADBLOCK → FIX

The wall: people reach for inheritance to share code and end up with fragile deep hierarchies (the classic "banana → gorilla → jungle" problem — you wanted one method, you got the world). The fix the field settled on: composition over inheritance + dependency injection — pass collaborators in, don't subclass to get them. Second gotcha: over-abstracting too early; add the interface when you have two implementations, not before.

05KEY IDEAS / HINTS
  • @dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True) = immutable + memory-tight.
  • __post_init__ validates invariants at construction.
  • The five shape tools now in hand: TypedDict (static dict) · dataclass (object) · Pydantic (validated) · NamedTuple (immutable tuple) · Protocol (interface).

10 ○ UPCOMING

Decorators, context managers and generators

0 / 170 XP
CUTOFF TARGET
a working @retry_on_transient, a reconciliation_run context manager and a streaming stream_records generator, all covered by passing tests.
01REVIEW

Answer each aloud or on paper before you look anything up. A miss goes into error-log.md with one line of correction.

02CONCEPT

Three tools make Python code read like the problem. A decorator wraps a function to add behaviour (retry, cache, timing) without editing it. A context manager (with) guarantees cleanup — commit on success, roll back on error. A generator (yield) produces values one at a time, so a 10 GB file costs the memory of one row. Pipelines use all three constantly.

03ALTERNATIVES
  • Decorator — behavior that wraps whole functions uniformly (retry/cache/log).
  • Context manager — behavior bracketing a block with guaranteed cleanup (resources, transactions).
  • Plain try/finally — fine for one-off cleanup; promote to a context manager when you repeat it.
  • Middleware (web frameworks) — when the cross-cutting concern spans requests, not functions.
04ROADBLOCK → FIX

Two classic walls: (1) a decorator clobbers the wrapped function's name/docstring → tooling and tracebacks get confusing. Fix: @functools.wraps(fn) on the wrapper. (2) Writing a parameterized decorator and getting lost in the nesting (TypeError: got multiple values). Fix: remember it's three layers — args → decorator(fn) → wrapper(*a, **kw) — and write them outside-in.

05KEY IDEAS / HINTS
  • itertools.batched (3.12+) re-chunks a stream into fixed batches.
  • groupby on a sorted stream = SQL-style aggregation without loading all rows.
  • Pull-based iteration is backpressure — the consumer sets the pace.

  • Real Python: Generators — extract: lazy eval + memory profile.

pytest and mocking: fast tests with no real I/O

0 / 170 XP
CUTOFF TARGET
pytest -q runs a suite with fixtures and parametrize, and the retry and time-based logic is tested with zero real I/O and zero real sleeping.
01REVIEW

Answer each aloud or on paper before you look anything up. A miss goes into error-log.md with one line of correction.

02CONCEPT

pytest is the default Python test framework: plain assert, fixtures for shared setup and parametrize to run one test body over many inputs. Tests are what let you change code without fear. A mock replaces a real dependency (network, clock, database) so a test runs fast and the same way every time. The rule: mock at the boundary you own, not deep inside someone else's library.

03ALTERNATIVES
  • pytest — the default for app/library testing; rich plugin ecosystem.
  • unittest (stdlib) — pick only when you can't add deps, or you're in a codebase already using it.
  • doctest — tiny executable examples in docstrings; nice for docs, not a real suite.
  • fixtures vs plain setup — use fixtures when setup is shared/expensive; a local object is fine for one test.
04ROADBLOCK → FIX

The classic wall: tests that pass alone but fail together (or vice-versa) because of shared state / order dependence. The fix the community reaches for: function-scoped fixtures (fresh state per test), tmp_path for files, and never mutating module-level globals in tests. Second gotcha: slow suites — mark slow ones (@pytest.mark.slow) and keep the default run fast.

05KEY IDEAS / HINTS
  • mocker.patch("pkg.mod.dep") (pytest-mock) is cleaner than nested with patch.
  • freezegun.freeze_time(...) pins datetime.now(); patch sleep so backoff tests are instant.
  • Assert behavior (final state) over implementation (exact calls) where you can.

  • unittest.mock — extract: patch, MagicMock, side_effect.

12 ○ UPCOMING

asyncio, threads, processes and the GIL

0 / 170 XP
CUTOFF TARGET
Sentinel-Lite fetches source and truth concurrently with asyncio, and you can say when to use asyncio, threads or processes, backed by a measured demo.
01REVIEW

Answer each aloud or on paper before you look anything up. A miss goes into error-log.md with one line of correction.

02CONCEPT

Concurrency answers one question: what is the program waiting on? Waiting on the network or disk (I/O-bound): asyncio or threads help, because the program idles most of the time. Burning CPU (CPU-bound): the GIL lets only one thread run Python bytecode at a time, so threads do not speed it up and you use processes. asyncio runs many tasks on one thread by switching at every await; one blocking call inside a coroutine stalls everything.

03ALTERNATIVES
  • asyncio — high-concurrency I/O, one thread, low overhead.
  • ThreadPoolExecutor — I/O-bound work using blocking libraries.
  • ProcessPoolExecutor / multiprocessing — CPU-bound (parsing/crunching millions of rows): real parallelism, at the cost of IPC/serialization.
  • A real distributed engine (Spark, Days 26–27) — when data exceeds one machine.
04ROADBLOCK → FIX

The classic trap: calling a blocking function inside async code (e.g. requests.get, time.sleep) freezes the whole event loop — async "doesn't work" and nobody knows why. Fixes: use async-native libs (httpx, asyncio.sleep), or push blocking calls to asyncio.to_thread(...). Second gotcha: forgetting to await (you get a coroutine object, not a result) — a warning the linter will flag.

05KEY IDEAS / HINTS
  • Decision tree: I/O-bound + async libs → asyncio; I/O-bound + blocking libs → threads; CPU-bound → processes.
  • concurrent.futures gives one API (ThreadPoolExecutor/ProcessPoolExecutor) to swap between them.
06READ
  • Real Python: Async IO — extract: event loop, coroutine vs task, gather.
  • Real Python: Python GIL — extract: what it locks, why it exists.

13 ○ UPCOMING

Resilience: backoff, circuit breaker, idempotency

0 / 170 XP
CUTOFF TARGET
Sentinel-Lite survives a flapping dependency: it retries with backoff, trips a circuit breaker, and re-running a batch changes nothing.
01REVIEW

Answer each aloud or on paper before you look anything up. A miss goes into error-log.md with one line of correction.

02CONCEPT

Production systems assume dependencies fail, and "it failed halfway and we ran it again" is a daily event at scale. Three patterns make that safe. Retry with exponential backoff and jitter rides out short blips. A circuit breaker stops hammering a dead dependency, fails fast, then probes for recovery. Idempotency makes a repeated run harmless — the same lesson as Day 4, now in code. Optional extra (15 minutes): one Hypothesis property test, "reconciling twice equals reconciling once".

03ALTERNATIVES
  • tenacity — declarative retry/backoff via decorator. Default over hand-rolled loops.
  • Circuit breaker (e.g. pybreaker) — when a dependency can stay down; protects it from a retry storm and you from cascading latency.
  • Idempotency key + dedup — when re-delivery is possible (almost always in distributed systems).
  • DLQ + replay — when some items can't be processed now but shouldn't block the batch.
04ROADBLOCK → FIX

The classic failure: retry storms — everything retries in lockstep and synchronized-hammers the recovering service into staying down (the "thundering herd"). Fix: jitter (randomize backoff) + a circuit breaker + a retry budget/cap. Second gotcha: retrying a non-idempotent write doubles data (anyone who has operated a CDC pipeline has met this) — fix with an idempotency key or an upsert/MERGE keyed on a natural id.

05KEY IDEAS / HINTS
  • Retry only transient errors; never retry a validation/4xx-type error.
  • Circuit breaker states: closed → (failures) open → (cooldown) half-open → closed.
  • Idempotency = "apply once" semantics even under at-least-once delivery.
06READ
  • tenacity docs — extract: stop, wait, retry, jitter.
  • Stripe: Idempotency + skim a circuit-breaker write-up — extract: idempotency keys, breaker states.

15 ○ UPCOMING

Hashmaps, frequency and strings

0 / 170 XP
CUTOFF TARGET
on each problem, say the trigger phrase that flags "hashmap," then state "O(n)/O(n)" before coding.
01REVIEW

Answer each aloud or on paper before you look anything up. A miss goes into error-log.md with one line of correction.

02CONCEPT

A dict gives O(1) average lookup/insert. The move: replace an O(n²) "search for a matching/related element" with one pass that remembers what it has already seen (or counts occurrences).

03ALTERNATIVES
  • Words: "have we seen," "count / frequency / how many times," "duplicate," "anagram / grouping," "pair that sums to," "first unique."
  • Constraint signal: n is large (10⁴–10⁶) so O(n²) is too slow → you need O(n).
  • Shape: "for each element, is there another element with property X?" → store what you've seen keyed by X.
04ALTERNATIVES

Hashmap when you need existence/count by key and order doesn't matter. Need sorted order → sort first (O(n log n)). Keys are a small fixed range (e.g. 26 letters) → a fixed array beats a dict. Need order and lookup → dict preserves insertion order (3.7+).

05ROADBLOCK → FIX

Reaching for a nested loop and timing out → store-as-you-go so the match is a lookup. KeyError → use dict.get(k, default), defaultdict, or Counter. Matching an element with itself → check-before-insert.

06THOUGHT PROCESS (REPEATABLE STEPS)
  1. Ask: "for each item, what related item am I looking for?" Name it (the complement, the same key, the count).
  2. Choose the key (the thing you look up) and the value (index, count, or list).
  3. One pass: check the map first (is the thing I need already here?), then add the current item. Order matters — check before insert to avoid matching yourself.
  4. State complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space.

Worked mini-example — Two Sum. "Return indices of two numbers that add to target." Trigger = "two numbers that add to" → looking for a complement. Key = the number, value = its index. Walk the array: for num, the related item is target - num; check if target - num is in the map → if yes, return both indices; then store num → index. One pass, O(n)/O(n). The naïve nested loop is O(n²) — the map removes the inner loop.

07SQL BRIDGE

Hashmap = GROUP BY + hash aggregate. Counter(items) ≈ SELECT item, COUNT(*) GROUP BY item. Building a lookup dict ≈ a hash join's build phase.

Two pointers and sliding window

0 / 170 XP
CUTOFF TARGET
on sight, classify a problem as converging-two-pointers, fast/slow, or sliding-window — and say why.
01REVIEW

Answer each aloud or on paper before you look anything up. A miss goes into error-log.md with one line of correction.

02CONCEPT

Two indices walk a sequence with O(1) extra space instead of nested loops. Sliding window is the variable-width variant: expand right to include elements, shrink left to restore a constraint — built for "longest/shortest contiguous run where X."

03ALTERNATIVES
  • Two pointers: "sorted array," "pair/triplet that sums to," "is it a palindrome," "remove duplicates in place," "max area / container."
  • Sliding window: "contiguous subarray/substring," "longest/shortest … such that," "at most K," "without repeating."
  • Fast/slow: "cycle," "find the middle," "happy number."
  • Constraint signal: the answer is a contiguous run, or the array is sorted, and n is large → O(n) needed.
04ALTERNATIVES

Two pointers (converging) → sorted, find a pair/triplet. Sliding window → contiguous run under a constraint. Fast/slow → cycle / middle. If the subarray isn't contiguous or you need all-pairs → hashmap or DP instead.

05ROADBLOCK → FIX

Off-by-one / wrong answers from mishandling when to shrink → use the fixed template (expand always; while violated, shrink; record when valid) and write the invariant as a comment. Forgetting to update the aggregate when shrinking → remove from the window exactly what you added.

06THOUGHT PROCESS (SLIDING WINDOW STEPS)
  1. Confirm it's contiguous + has a constraint you can test as you grow.
  2. Init left = 0, a window aggregate (sum / count / a Counter), and best.
  3. For each right: add nums[right] to the window.
  4. while the window violates the constraint: remove nums[left], left += 1.
  5. The window is now valid → update best. (Invariant: window is always valid after the while.)
  6. Complexity: each element enters and leaves once → O(n).

Worked mini-example — Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters. Trigger = "longest substring … without repeating" = contiguous + constraint ("no repeats"). Window = a set/Counter of chars in [left, right]. Expand right, adding the char. If it's now a duplicate, shrink from left (removing chars) until the duplicate is gone — invariant restored. Record right - left + 1 as a candidate max at each valid step. Each index moves forward only → O(n)/O(k).

07SQL BRIDGE

Sliding window = a running aggregate over a moving range (SUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY t ROWS BETWEEN ...)). Two-pointer on sorted data = a merge join.

17 ○ UPCOMING

Stacks, queues and the monotonic stack

0 / 170 XP
CUTOFF TARGET
see "matching/nesting" → stack, "next greater/smaller" → monotonic stack, instantly.
01REVIEW

Answer each aloud or on paper before you look anything up. A miss goes into error-log.md with one line of correction.

02CONCEPT

A stack (LIFO) holds "the most recent unresolved thing" — brackets, undo, call frames. A monotonic stack keeps its contents sorted so it can answer "next greater/smaller element" in O(n). A queue/deque (FIFO) drives BFS and sliding-window-max.

03ALTERNATIVES
  • Stack: "valid parentheses / balanced," "nesting," "undo," "evaluate expression," "most recent."
  • Monotonic stack: "next greater / warmer / larger element," "days until," "previous smaller," "largest rectangle."
  • Queue/deque: "level order," "shortest steps," "sliding window maximum."
  • Constraint signal: you'd otherwise compare each element to others to its right → O(n²); monotonic stack makes it O(n).
04ALTERNATIVES

Stack → nesting/matching/"most recent." Monotonic stack → next-greater/smaller, spans. Queue/deque → BFS, window-max, producer/consumer. Need random access by index → that's an array, not a stack.

05ROADBLOCK → FIX

Not seeing the monotonic-stack case → pattern-match the phrase "next greater/smaller to the right," push indices, pop while beaten. Using a list as a queue with .pop(0) (O(n)) → use collections.deque (O(1) both ends).

06THOUGHT PROCESS (MONOTONIC STACK STEPS)
  1. Spot "for each element, find the next element to the right that is greater/smaller."
  2. Keep a stack of indices whose answers aren't resolved yet.
  3. For each new index i: while stack non-empty and nums[i] beats nums[stack[-1]] → pop, and i is that popped index's answer.
  4. Push i. Anything left on the stack at the end has no answer (default 0/-1).
  5. Each index pushed/popped once → O(n).

Worked mini-example — Daily Temperatures. "For each day, how many days until a warmer one?" Trigger = "next warmer to the right." Looks like nested loops (O(n²)) but is monotonic-stack. Stack holds indices of days awaiting a warmer day. For day i: while the current temp > temp at stack[-1], pop index j and set answer[j] = i - j. Push i. O(n)/O(n).

07SQL BRIDGE

"Next greater element" ≈ LEAD()/LAG() reasoning over an ordering. Nesting ≈ a recursive CTE walking a hierarchy.

Binary search, including on the answer

0 / 170 XP
CUTOFF TARGET
recognize plain binary search and "binary-search-the-answer," and write one bug-free template.
01REVIEW

Answer each aloud or on paper before you look anything up. A miss goes into error-log.md with one line of correction.

02CONCEPT

Halve a sorted or monotonic space each step → O(log n). The senior move is "search the answer": when feasibility of a candidate value is monotonic (if X works, anything bigger works), binary-search the value range itself.

03ALTERNATIVES
  • Plain: "sorted array," "find target / position," "rotated sorted."
  • On the answer: "minimum/maximum value such that …," "smallest capacity / speed / days to …," and you can write a yes/no feasible(x) test that's monotonic.
  • Constraint signal: huge value range (e.g. 1…10⁹) but a cheap feasibility check → O(log(range)·check).
04ALTERNATIVES

Sorted data + lookup → plain binary search. Monotonic predicate over a numeric range → search the answer. Repeated k-th smallest → heap. Unsorted single lookup → hashmap (don't sort just to search once).

05ROADBLOCK → FIX

Off-by-one / infinite loops → commit to one template (half-open [lo, hi), while lo < hi, mid=(lo+hi)//2) and never improvise; use bisect for plain lookups. Missing that the answer is the monotonic thing → always ask "can I write a monotonic feasible(x)?"

06THOUGHT PROCESS (SEARCH-THE-ANSWER STEPS)
  1. Define feasible(x) returning True/False, and confirm it's monotonic (False…False, True…True).
  2. Set lo/hi to the value range bounds.
  3. while lo < hi: mid = (lo + hi)//2; if feasible(mid): hi = mid else: lo = mid + 1.
  4. lo is the boundary — the smallest feasible value.
  5. Complexity: O(log(range) × cost of feasible).

Worked mini-example — Koko Eating Bananas. "Min eating speed to finish in H hours." Trigger = "minimum speed such that … within a limit." feasible(speed) = total hours at that speed ≤ H — monotonic (faster always finishes sooner). Binary-search speed in [1, max(pile)]; keep the smallest feasible. The array isn't what's sorted — the answer space is monotonic. That recognition is the whole point.

07SQL BRIDGE

Like an index seek vs a scan — log-time targeted lookup instead of reading everything.

08READ

0 / 170 XP
CUTOFF TARGET
see "top-k / k-th / streaming min-max" → heap, and "intervals / scheduling" → sort-by-start sweep.
01REVIEW

Answer each aloud or on paper before you look anything up. A miss goes into error-log.md with one line of correction.

02CONCEPT

A heap (priority queue) gives O(log n) push/pop with O(1) peek at the min — for "k largest," "merge k sorted," running median. Interval problems (merge/overlap/scheduling) start with "sort by start, then sweep," often with a min-heap of end-times.

03ALTERNATIVES
  • Heap: "top K," "k-th largest/smallest," "K closest," "merge K sorted," "running/median," "schedule by priority."
  • Intervals: "merge overlapping," "meeting rooms," "can attend all," "minimum number of … to cover," "\[start, end\] pairs."
  • Constraint signal (heap): you need the best-k, not a full sort → O(n log k) beats O(n log n). Streaming data → can't sort once.
04ALTERNATIVES

Heap → top-k / k-th / streaming min-max / k-way merge. Full sort → when you need everything ordered. Intervals → sort + sweep; min-heap of ends for resource-count.

05ROADBLOCK → FIX

heapq is min-heap only → push negated values for a max-heap; push (priority, tiebreaker, item) tuples so comparisons never blow up on un-orderable objects. Intervals: forgetting to sort first, or fumbling touching intervals → sort by start and decide < vs <= explicitly.

06THOUGHT PROCESS — INTERVALS STEPS

Sort by start; walk; if the current interval overlaps the last kept one (start <= prev_end), merge (extend end); else start a new one. For "rooms needed," push end-times to a min-heap and pop whenever a new start ≥ the smallest end.

Worked mini-example — Merge Intervals. Trigger = "merge overlapping \[start,end\]." Sort by start (the universal first move). Walk: keep current; if next.start <= current.end they overlap → current.end = max(current.end, next.end); else push current and set current = next. Sort dominates → O(n log n).

07SQL BRIDGE

Top-k heap ≈ ORDER BY … LIMIT k (but streaming). K-way merge ≈ merging sorted partitions. Intervals ≈ time-range reconciliation — exactly your TimeAllocations/TimePunches overlap logic.

CUTOFF TARGET

01REVIEW

Answer each aloud or on paper before you look anything up. A miss goes into error-log.md with one line of correction.

02CONCEPT

Trees/graphs model hierarchy and relationships. DFS (deep; recursion or an explicit stack) and BFS (wide; a queue) are the two traversals everything builds on — paths, components, levels, ordering.

03ALTERNATIVES
  • Graph/tree at all: "grid / matrix of cells," "connected," "network," "tree," "nodes and edges," "dependencies," "regions / islands."
  • BFS specifically: "shortest path / fewest steps" on an unweighted graph, or "level by level."
  • DFS specifically: "does a path exist," "all paths," "explore fully," "topological / ordering," "flood fill."
  • Constraint signal: input is a grid, tree, adjacency list, or "n items with dependencies."
04ALTERNATIVES

BFS → shortest unweighted path, level-order. DFS → path existence, full exploration, topo sort, backtracking. Weighted shortest path → Dijkstra (heap). Connectivity under unions → Union-Find. DAG cycle detection → DFS colors or Kahn's topo sort.

05ROADBLOCK → FIX

Infinite loop / re-processing → you forgot visited, or marked it too late (mark on enqueue/entry). Recursion depth blowup on deep input → convert DFS to an explicit stack. Picking the wrong traversal → "shortest" on unweighted = BFS, reflexively.

06THOUGHT PROCESS (STEPS)
  1. Identify nodes and edges (for a grid: each cell is a node; neighbors are up/down/left/right).
  2. Pick traversal: shortest-unweighted → BFS; existence / full exploration / ordering → DFS.
  3. Keep a visited set; mark visited when you enqueue (BFS) or on entry (DFS).
  4. BFS: queue, pop front, push unvisited neighbors, track depth per level. DFS: recurse (or stack), process node, recurse neighbors.
  5. Complexity: O(V + E) time, O(V) space.

Worked mini-example — Number of Islands. Trigger = "grid + connected regions of land." Nodes = cells; edges = 4-directional neighbors. Count = number of connected components. Loop every cell; when you hit unvisited land, increment the count and DFS/BFS to mark the whole island visited so you don't recount it. Each cell visited once → O(rows·cols).

07SQL BRIDGE

DAG traversal = dbt/Airflow dependency order. Recursive CTE = DFS/BFS over a hierarchy. "Number of Islands" = connected components.

02CONCEPT

Parquet stores data by column in row groups, with min/max statistics per column chunk, so an engine reads only the columns and row groups it needs. A table format (Iceberg, Delta Lake, Hudi) adds a metadata layer on top of those files so a folder of files behaves like a table: atomic commits, a schema, snapshots and hidden partitioning. Plain "files in a folder" cannot do safe concurrent writes, time travel or schema evolution.

03ALTERNATIVES

Iceberg → open, engine-agnostic, strong evolution. Delta Lake → Databricks-native. Hudi → upsert/CDC-first heritage. Plain Hive tables → legacy, avoid.

Keep a two-column map in your notes (Iceberg term ↔ Delta term). Interviewers switch dialects mid-question.

The Iceberg Spark runtime jar must match your Spark + Scala version or you get cryptic ClassNotFound/catalog errors → pin the exact iceberg-spark-runtime-<spark>_<scala> and configure the catalog explicitly. Be deliberate about which catalog (Hadoop/REST/Glue) owns the table.

05KEY IDEAS / HINTS

Row groups + column stats (min/max per chunk) enable predicate pushdown ("skip this chunk"). pyarrow.parquet to inspect metadata.

ACID, snapshots, time travel and schema evolution

0 / 170 XP
CUTOFF TARGET
make three commits, read each snapshot by id and by timestamp, roll back, then rename a column and change the partition spec while old snapshots still read correctly.
01REVIEW

Answer each aloud or on paper before you look anything up. A miss goes into error-log.md with one line of correction.

02CONCEPT

Table-format commits are atomic and create immutable snapshots: a reader sees one consistent version while a writer works, and you can query or roll back to any earlier state ("time travel"). You use it to recover from a bad write, reproduce a report "as of" a date, and run readers and writers together safely. Schema and partition evolution work through metadata, not rewrites: columns are tracked by id, so a rename is safe, and a new partition spec applies only to new writes.

03ALTERNATIVES
  • Snapshot isolation (Iceberg and Delta default) — readers are untouched by in-flight writes; fits analytics.
  • Serializable — stops write skew between concurrent writers; rarer in batch, and costlier.
  • Time travel vs backups — time travel is short-term and bounded by snapshot retention; a backup is for disaster recovery.
04ROADBLOCK → FIX

The Hive trap: assuming a rename rewrites or breaks history — in Iceberg it's metadata-only and safe because of field IDs. Changing a partition spec doesn't re-partition old data (only new writes) → plan a compaction/rewrite if you need old data re-laid-out.

05KEY IDEAS / HINTS

Field IDs make rename safe. Hidden partitioning means queries don't hardcode partition columns — you can evolve them.

  • Time travel: VERSION AS OF / TIMESTAMP AS OF in Spark SQL; roll back with the table procedures, not by deleting files.
06READ
  • Iceberg Spark queries — extract: time travel by snapshot id and by timestamp, and the metadata tables.
  • Iceberg evolution — extract: why a rename is safe (field IDs) and what a partition-spec change does not rewrite.

CDC into the lakehouse with MERGE

0 / 170 XP
CUTOFF TARGET

01REVIEW

Answer each aloud or on paper before you look anything up. A miss goes into error-log.md with one line of correction.

02CONCEPT

MERGE INTO upserts change-data: match on a key, update/delete/insert accordingly — the lakehouse version of the CDC pipelines that feed most enterprise warehouses. COW rewrites whole files on update (fast reads, slow writes); MOR writes delete/update deltas merged at read time (fast writes, slower reads). This is the day that connects existing warehouse and ETL experience to the lakehouse stack — for anyone coming from a SQL or ETL background, that bridge is the single biggest interview asset.

03ALTERNATIVES

COW → read-heavy, infrequent updates (BI tables). MOR → write/update-heavy, streaming CDC — at the cost of read-time merge + compaction. Choosing per-table is a senior signal.

04ROADBLOCK → FIX

The CDC feed must carry the delete. If the feed collapses a hard-deleted row into nothing, MERGE has no way to remove it and the target keeps a ghost row. Fix: emit an op-type (I/U/D) on every change and handle WHEN MATCHED AND op = 'D' THEN DELETE. Second wall: merge-on-read without compaction makes reads slower every day; schedule compaction (Day 25). This is the Day 4 MERGE guard at lakehouse scale: dedup the batch, guard on the change sequence, then merge.

05KEY IDEAS / HINTS

MERGE INTO t USING changes ON t.key=changes.key WHEN MATCHED AND op='D' THEN DELETE WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE ... WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT .... Write your copy-on-write vs merge-on-read decision rule in one sentence in error-log.md.

Table maintenance: compaction, expiry, and the Delta equivalents

0 / 170 XP
CUTOFF TARGET
create the small-files problem, run compaction, re-measure file count and scan time, then expire old snapshots.
01REVIEW

Answer each aloud or on paper before you look anything up. A miss goes into error-log.md with one line of correction.

02CONCEPT

Lakehouse tables need housekeeping. Compaction turns many small files into a few large ones, snapshot expiration bounds metadata and storage, and orphan-file cleanup removes files no snapshot references. Streaming and CDC writes create small files and endless snapshots that quietly slow reads and raise cost. Interviewers ask this as "your table got slower every week — why, and what do you schedule?"

03ALTERNATIVES

rewrite_data_files (compaction) → small files. expire_snapshots → bound metadata/storage. rewrite_manifests → manifest bloat. Schedule by write rate (MOR needs it more).

  • Delta equivalents — OPTIMIZE ≈ compaction, VACUUM ≈ expire snapshots plus orphan cleanup, ZORDER ≈ sort-order clustering.
04ROADBLOCK → FIX

Compaction competes with writers and is costly run naively → compact incrementally (recent partitions), schedule off-peak, tune target file size. Expiring snapshots too aggressively kills time-travel you still need → set retention from your actual RPO.

05KEY IDEAS / HINTS

Decide the 3 metrics you'd alert on (file count/size, snapshot count, commit latency) — they become capstone dashboard panels.

26 ○ UPCOMING

PySpark: lazy execution, the shuffle and skew

0 / 170 XP
CUTOFF TARGET
rewrite a SQL transform as a PySpark DataFrame job against Iceberg, read its physical plan, and point at the shuffle.
01REVIEW

Answer each aloud or on paper before you look anything up. A miss goes into error-log.md with one line of correction.

02CONCEPT

Spark distributes a computation across a cluster: a DataFrame is a logical description, and Spark builds an optimized physical plan that runs in parallel across partitions. Transformations are lazy (they just build the plan); an action (count, write, collect) triggers execution. The expensive thing is the shuffle — moving data across the network to group/join by key. Engineers reach for Spark when data outgrows one machine; your SQL instincts transfer directly (it's SQL-shaped), but you now reason about partitions and shuffles the way you reason about indexes and scans.

03ALTERNATIVES

Spark → data > one machine, or you need a cluster. DuckDB/Polars → single-node analytics, often faster up to ~100GB and far simpler — pick first if it fits. Pandas → small data, prototyping. SQL-in-warehouse (Snowflake/BigQuery) → when the warehouse is the compute. Senior signal: not reaching for Spark when DuckDB would do.

04ROADBLOCK → FIX

The #1 Spark pain: data skew — one key has most of the rows, so one task runs forever while others finish (the straggler). You'll see it as a single slow task in the UI. Fixes the field uses: salt the hot key, broadcast the small side of a join, or repartition by a better key. Second gotcha: calling .collect() on a huge DataFrame pulls it all to the driver → OOM; aggregate first, collect small.

05KEY IDEAS / HINTS
  • Narrow transforms (map/filter) = no shuffle. Wide transforms (groupBy/join/distinct) = shuffle.
  • df.explain() shows the physical plan — look for Exchange (= a shuffle).
  • Broadcast join (broadcast(small_df)) avoids shuffling the big side.

01REVIEW

Answer each aloud or on paper before you look anything up. A miss goes into error-log.md with one line of correction.

02CONCEPT

Structured Streaming treats a stream as an unbounded table processed in micro-batches — same DataFrame API as batch, so one mental model covers both. Engineers use it for near-real-time pipelines (CDC ingestion, metrics, alerting). The two ideas that make it correct: checkpointing (it remembers offsets so a restart resumes exactly where it left off) and idempotent sinks (writing the same micro-batch twice doesn't double data) → together they give exactly-once. This is your "real-time systems" goal landing on the lakehouse.

03ALTERNATIVES

Spark Structured Streaming → micro-batch, unifies with your batch code, lakehouse sink. Flink → true record-at-a-time, lower latency, richer state — pick when sub-second + complex event-time logic matters. Kafka Streams → JVM apps close to Kafka. Plain batch on a schedule → when minutes-to-hours latency is fine (often it is — don't stream by default).

04ROADBLOCK → FIX

The classic trap: deleting or losing the checkpoint → on restart the job reprocesses from the beginning (or skips data), breaking exactly-once. Fix: treat the checkpoint dir as sacred state, one per query, never share or hand-edit it. Second gotcha: tiny micro-batches → the small-files problem on the Iceberg side; tune trigger interval + compact (Day 25).

05KEY IDEAS / HINTS
  • Output modes: append / update / complete — pick by whether aggregates change.
  • trigger(processingTime=...) controls batch cadence; availableNow drains a backlog.
  • Watermarks bound state for event-time aggregations (drop data later than the watermark).

02CONCEPT

dbt lets you build transformations as SELECT statements (models) that it turns into tables/views, with dependencies expressed via ref() so dbt computes the build DAG and runs them in order. Engineers love it because it brings software practices to SQL: version control, testing, documentation, and incremental builds. It's the de-facto transformation layer (the "T" in ELT) — and it plays directly to your SQL strength while teaching the modern workflow around it.

03ALTERNATIVES

dbt → SQL-centric transformations with tests + lineage (the default "T"). Hand-written Spark/SQL jobs → when logic is too imperative for SQL. SQLMesh → a newer dbt alternative with stronger incremental/virtual-environment semantics — worth name-dropping. Materialized views in the warehouse → simple cases.

04ROADBLOCK → FIX

The incremental-model trap: a naive incremental model double-counts or misses late-arriving rows. Fix: use is_incremental() with a proper filter on an updated-at watermark, and choose the right incremental_strategy (merge vs insert-overwrite) — merge keyed on your unique id is the safe default (the same MERGE idea as Day 24). Second gotcha: full-refresh accidentally in prod → guard it.

05KEY IDEAS / HINTS
  • Materializations: view (cheap, always fresh) · table (fast reads, rebuilt) · incremental (only new rows) · ephemeral (inlined CTE).

  • staging (clean/rename) → intermediate → marts (business-facing) is the standard layering.

02CONCEPT

Data quality testing asserts properties of data (not code): no nulls in a key, values in an allowed set, row counts in range, freshness within SLA. Data contracts make these expectations explicit and enforced at boundaries so a bad upstream change fails loud instead of silently corrupting downstream tables. Engineers treat this as the data equivalent of unit tests + types — it's exactly your Sentinel-Lite reconciliation instinct, now declarative and in the pipeline.

03ALTERNATIVES

dbt tests (generic + singular) → cheapest, lives with your models, default. Great Expectations → richer expectation suites + data docs, pick for heavier validation/profiling. Soda / Elementary → monitoring + anomaly detection over time. Pandera → DataFrame-level schema checks in Python/Spark. Pick the lightest that enforces the contract.

04ROADBLOCK → FIX

The trap: tests that warn but don't block → bad data flows downstream anyway and everyone ignores the warnings. Fix: make critical tests error-severity and wire them as a gate (pipeline stops, batch quarantined) — your "fail the run, quarantine the batch" pattern from Sentinel-Lite. Second gotcha: over-testing every column → noise; test keys, critical invariants, and freshness, not everything.

05KEY IDEAS / HINTS
  • dbt generic tests: not_null, unique, accepted_values, relationships (FK). Singular tests = a SELECT that should return zero rows.
  • Freshness: assert max(updated_at) within SLA.
  • A failing gate should quarantine the batch + emit a metric (ties to the Day 14 observability and the capstone dashboard).

Orchestration with Airflow (Dagster as a comparison)

0 / 170 XP
CUTOFF TARGET
your ingest → transform → quality gate → publish steps run as an Airflow DAG with a schedule, retries, and a backfill that is safe to repeat.
01REVIEW

Answer each aloud or on paper before you look anything up. A miss goes into error-log.md with one line of correction.

02CONCEPT

An orchestrator runs tasks in dependency order on a schedule, retries failures, and shows you what ran and what did not. Airflow is the common default: a DAG file declares tasks and dependencies, a scheduler creates runs per data interval, and workers execute them. The key habit is idempotent tasks: a task reads and writes the slice for its data interval (not "now"), so a retry or a backfill produces the same result.

03ALTERNATIVES
  • Airflow — the default in postings and interviews; big ecosystem, schedule-centric.
  • Dagster — asset-centric (you declare the tables, not the tasks); great lineage. Spend one hour on it for the comparison.
  • Prefect — Python-first, lighter to start.
  • Cloud-native — Step Functions, Azure Data Factory, Databricks Workflows: fewer servers to run, less portable.
  • Cron + a script — fine for one job; no retries, no visibility, no backfill.
04ROADBLOCK → FIX

Top-level code in a DAG file runs on every scheduler parse, so a database call at import time slows or breaks the whole scheduler. Keep the file light and do the work inside tasks. Second wall: using datetime.now() inside a task instead of the run's data interval, which makes a backfill write today's data into last month's partition. Third: passing big data through XCom — pass a path or a table name instead.

05KEY IDEAS / HINTS
  • Logical date and data interval: a run for 2026-01-05 processes the 2026-01-05 slice, whenever it executes.
  • catchup, max_active_runs, retries with exponential backoff, and pools for rate limits.
  • Sensors wait for something (a file, a partition); prefer deferrable sensors so they do not hold a worker slot.
  • A failed quality-gate task must stop the publish task: dependency, not hope.

The trap: column-level lineage is much harder than table-level, and naive setups only get table-level → you can't answer "which downstream column depends on this one." Second gotcha: catalog mismatch between engines (Spark vs Trino reading the same Iceberg tables) → standardize on a REST/Glue catalog both speak.

05KEY IDEAS / HINTS
  • Least privilege: grant roles, not people; read-only by default.

  • Retention is a rule per table, written down, and enforced by a job.
  • Lineage answers "what breaks if I change this column?"

36 ○ UPCOMING

Consistency, isolation, replication and consensus

0 / 170 XP
CUTOFF TARGET
explain CAP and PACELC correctly (the common version is wrong), place snapshot vs serializable isolation on the spectrum, and say in two sentences why consensus exists.
01REVIEW

Answer each aloud or on paper before you look anything up. A miss goes into error-log.md with one line of correction.

02CONCEPT

A distributed system cannot treat the network as reliable, so you choose what to give up when links fail. CAP says that during a network partition a system must pick consistency or availability; it says nothing about normal operation. PACELC adds the part interviewers care about: else (no partition), you still trade latency against consistency. Replication copies data to survive failures: leader-follower, multi-leader or leaderless quorums. When copies disagree about who the leader is (split brain), a consensus protocol such as Raft gets a majority to agree. Explain level is enough; you do not need to implement Raft.

03ALTERNATIVES

Sync replication → no data loss on failover, but higher write latency + lower availability (a slow follower blocks). Async → fast writes, but a failover can lose the last un-replicated writes (RPO > 0). Leaderless quorum → high availability + tunable, but you handle conflicts (LWW/CRDT). Multi-leader → multi-region writes, at the cost of conflict resolution.

04ROADBLOCK → FIX

The interview trap: reciting "CAP = pick 2 of 3." Fix: say "partitions are a given, so it's C-vs-A under partition; PACELC adds the latency-vs-consistency tradeoff in the normal case" — that one sentence signals you actually understand it. Second trap: conflating consistency (CAP) with isolation (ACID) — they're different axes; say so.

05KEY IDEAS / HINTS

Linearizable > sequential > causal > eventual. SNAPSHOT isolation allows write-skew; SERIALIZABLE doesn't. Read-your-writes, monotonic-reads are the "session guarantees" worth naming.

Partitioning, sharding and skew

0 / 170 XP
CUTOFF TARGET
choose a partition key for a given workload, and explain how you detect and fix a hot partition.
01REVIEW

Answer each aloud or on paper before you look anything up. A miss goes into error-log.md with one line of correction.

02CONCEPT

Partitioning (sharding) splits data across nodes so the system scales horizontally. The whole game is the partition key: a good one spreads load evenly and keeps related data together for efficient queries. Engineers obsess over this because the #1 scaling failure is a hot partition — one key (or range) gets most of the traffic and one node melts while others idle. You met the idea in table partitioning on Days 22–23; this is the distributed version.

03ALTERNATIVES

Hash partitioning → even spread, but kills range scans (adjacent keys scatter). Range partitioning → great range scans, but risks hot ranges (e.g. everything "today"). Composite (hash of a prefix + range) → balance. Consistent hashing → minimizes data movement when you add/remove nodes (vs naive hash % N which reshuffles everything).

04ROADBLOCK → FIX

The classic failure: a hot key (a celebrity user, a "today" timestamp, a NULL bucket). Detect it via per-partition metrics (one partition's QPS/latency dwarfs the rest; the metrics habit from Day 14). Fix: salt the hot key (append a random suffix to spread it, fan-in on read), or pick a higher-cardinality key. Second gotcha: choosing a key that forces cross-partition joins/transactions on the hot path → co-locate related data under the same key.

05KEY IDEAS / HINTS

hash % N reshuffles on resize → use consistent hashing/virtual nodes. Skew shows up as a single straggler task (the same thing you saw in Spark on Day 26). Rebalancing should move minimal data.

DDIA Ch 6 (Partitioning) — extract: key-range vs hash, rebalancing, request routing, hot spots.

38 ○ UPCOMING

Delivery semantics, idempotency and the outbox

0 / 170 XP
CUTOFF TARGET
explain why "exactly-once delivery" is a myth and how exactly-once processing is achieved.
01REVIEW

Answer each aloud or on paper before you look anything up. A miss goes into error-log.md with one line of correction.

02CONCEPT

In a distributed system you get at-most-once (may lose messages) or at-least-once (may duplicate); true exactly-once delivery is impossible (the two-generals problem). What engineers actually build is **exactly-once \*processing*** = at-least-once delivery + idempotent consumers (or dedup by an idempotency key) so duplicates have no effect. The transactional outbox*\* pattern solves the "update DB and publish event atomically" problem (write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction, relay it separately). This is the rigorous version of the resilience from Day 13 and the streaming exactly-once from Day 27, and the CDC hard-delete lesson from Day 24 generalized.

03ALTERNATIVES

At-most-once → telemetry where loss is fine and speed matters. At-least-once + idempotency → the default for anything that mutates state (almost everything). Outbox → when you must atomically change state and emit an event without a distributed transaction. Dual-write (update DB then publish) → tempting but broken (one can succeed while the other fails) — name why you avoid it.

04ROADBLOCK → FIX

The dual-write trap: "I'll update the DB, then publish to Kafka" → a crash between the two leaves them inconsistent. Fix: transactional outbox (or CDC from the database, the simplest fix when the source is a database (Debezium reads the log)). Second gotcha: idempotency keys that aren't actually unique per logical operation → use a natural business key + operation id; persist processed-ids to dedup.

05KEY IDEAS / HINTS

Idempotency = "apply once" even under retries/redelivery (upsert/MERGE on a natural key, as on Day 4). Outbox + a relay (or CDC) = atomic state-change + event. Kafka "exactly-once" = idempotent producer + transactions + a dedup'd consumer.

Backpressure, queues and flow control

0 / 170 XP
CUTOFF TARGET
explain backpressure, when to buffer, drop or block, and how a dead-letter queue plus replay fits a pipeline that fixes itself.
01REVIEW

Answer each aloud or on paper before you look anything up. A miss goes into error-log.md with one line of correction.

02CONCEPT

Backpressure is how a system protects itself when input arrives faster than it can process: it signals upstream to slow down (pull-based), or buffers/drops/blocks (push-based). Without it, queues grow unbounded → OOM/latency collapse → cascading failure. Engineers design flow control because every real pipeline eventually faces a burst. A dead-letter queue (DLQ) parks un-processable messages so one bad record doesn't block the stream, with replay to recover later — a building block of self-healing systems.

03ALTERNATIVES

Block (pull-based, bounded buffer) → when you can't lose data and upstream can slow (the generators from Day 10: pull = natural backpressure). Drop/sample → when fresh data matters more than completeness (metrics, telemetry). Buffer → smooths short bursts, but bounded or it's just deferred OOM. DLQ + replay → poison messages: isolate, alert, fix, replay.

04ROADBLOCK → FIX

The trap: an unbounded queue/buffer "to be safe" → it hides the problem until memory runs out under load (deferred catastrophe). Fix: bounded queues + an explicit policy (block/drop/DLQ) + a depth metric + alert. Second gotcha: a single poison message infinitely retried, blocking the whole partition → cap retries, route to DLQ, continue.

05KEY IDEAS / HINTS

Pull-based (consumer asks for more) gives backpressure for free; push-based needs explicit flow control. Little's Law (L = λW) sizes queues/concurrency. Queue depth + consumer lag are the metrics to alert on (Kafka consumer lag = your canary).

06READ

DDIA Ch 11 (messaging/streams + backpressure) — extract: message brokers, consumer lag, dropping vs buffering. Skim Reactive Streams backpressure — extract: the pull-based idea.

Fault tolerance and self-healing pipelines

0 / 170 XP
CUTOFF TARGET
design a pipeline that detects its own failures and recovers without a human, naming every pattern that does the work.
01REVIEW

Answer each aloud or on paper before you look anything up. A miss goes into error-log.md with one line of correction.

02CONCEPT

Fault tolerance = the system keeps working (possibly degraded) despite component failures; self-healing = it detects and recovers automatically. This pulls the last few days together: systems that recover without a human in the loop. The toolkit, now assembled: health checks + restarts, retries + backoff + jitter and circuit breakers (Day 13), idempotency + outbox (Day 38), DLQ + replay (Day 39), bulkheads (isolate failures), graceful degradation, and the reconciliation loop (Sentinel-Lite itself — detect drift from source-of-truth, auto-remediate).

03ALTERNATIVES

Retry → transient faults. Circuit breaker → a dependency that can stay down (stop the bleeding). Bulkhead → isolate so one failure doesn't sink everything (separate pools/queues). Graceful degradation → serve stale/partial rather than nothing. Reconciliation/control loop → the strongest form: continuously detect divergence and self-correct (a drift-triggered retrain, a data reconciliation job). Self-healing isn't free — it adds complexity; name when a human-in-the-loop alert is the right call instead.

04ROADBLOCK → FIX

The trap: "self-healing" that masks real problems — auto-retry hides a systemic bug, auto-remediation silently corrupts data. Fix: every automated recovery emits a metric + leaves an audit trail (you can't heal what you can't see; see the observability work on Day 14), and dangerous remediations quarantine + alert rather than guess. Second gotcha: no idempotency → self-healing retries double-apply (the failure mode behind the CDC MERGE on Day 24).

05KEY IDEAS / HINTS

The control-loop pattern (observe → diff vs desired → act) is what Kubernetes and your reconciliation service share — that's the senior framing of "self-healing." Bulkhead = the Titanic's compartments. Degradation > outage.
