Tokens, context windows and sampling

0 / 170 XP
CUTOFF TARGET
count tokens for different kinds of text, explain why cost and context limits are token limits, and show how temperature changes real output.
01REVIEW

Answer each aloud or on paper before you look anything up. A miss goes into error-log.md with one line of correction.

02CONCEPT

An LLM reads and writes tokens (word pieces), not words. Prices, speed and limits are all counted in tokens: input, output, and the context window, the most tokens the model can see at once (prompt plus answer). At each step the model produces a probability distribution over the next token and sampling picks from it. Temperature reshapes the distribution (low is predictable, high is varied), top-p keeps the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to p, and top-k keeps the k most likely. Temperature 0 is close to deterministic, not guaranteed identical.

03ALTERNATIVES
  • Low temperature vs higher — extraction, classification and SQL generation want low; brainstorming wants higher.
  • Top-p vs top-k — both trim the unlikely tail; change one at a time.
  • Long context vs retrieval — stuffing everything into the window costs more, slows responses and is less reliable in the middle; retrieval sends only what matters (Day 50).
  • Tokenizers differ by model family — counts from one do not match another.
04ROADBLOCK → FIX

Surprise cost and latency: a long system prompt plus chat history is re-sent on every call, so tokens balloon. Fix: log tokens in and out on every call, trim history, and cache stable prefixes. Second wall: "the model forgot." The early text fell out of the context window. The fix is summarizing or retrieving, not a bigger prompt.

05KEY IDEAS / HINTS
  • Rough rule: 1 token ≈ ¾ of an English word. Code, numbers and non-English text use more.
  • Cost = input tokens × input price + output tokens × output price; output usually costs more per token.
  • "Lost in the middle": details in the middle of a long prompt are recalled less reliably than the start or end.
06READ
  • OpenAI tokenizer tool — extract: paste English, code, JSON and another language; compare counts.
  • Karpathy — Intro to Large Language Models (first 25 min) — extract: next-token prediction and what training produces.

44 ○ UPCOMING

Attention and the transformer, at interview depth

0 / 170 XP
CUTOFF TARGET
explain self-attention, positional information and encoder vs decoder in under three minutes, with one small attention example computed by hand.
01REVIEW

Answer each aloud or on paper before you look anything up. A miss goes into error-log.md with one line of correction.

02CONCEPT

Self-attention lets every token look at every other token and decide how much of each to use. For each token the model makes a query, a key and a value; the weights are softmax(Q·Kᵀ / √d) and the output is the weighted sum of the values. Several heads run in parallel, and attention alone ignores order, so position information is added. A transformer block adds a feed-forward layer, residual connections and normalization, and many blocks are stacked. Encoder models read the input in both directions (embeddings, classification). Decoder models predict the next token using only earlier ones, which a causal mask enforces (most chat LLMs). Encoder-decoder models map one sequence to another (translation, summarization).

03ALTERNATIVES
  • Encoder vs decoder vs encoder-decoder — embeddings and rerankers use encoders; chat, generation and tool use use decoders; classic sequence-to-sequence uses encoder-decoder.
  • Transformer vs RNN — transformers train in parallel and handle long-range links better; RNNs process step by step.
  • Dense vs mixture-of-experts — only some experts run per token, so each token is cheaper while the total weights are larger.
04ROADBLOCK → FIX

Memorizing the formula without the reasons. Interviewers ask "why divide by √d?" (without it, dot products grow with dimension and push the softmax into a saturated range with tiny gradients) and "why a causal mask?" (so a token cannot see the future it is trying to predict). Fix: explain each piece by the problem it solves.

05KEY IDEAS / HINTS
  • Attention cost grows with the square of context length, because every token pair is compared.
  • KV cache: generation stores past keys and values so it does not recompute them; it trades memory for speed, and long contexts make it large.
  • Latency has two parts: prefill (process the prompt, parallel) and decode (one token at a time, sequential).
06READ
  • Jay Alammar — The Illustrated Transformer — extract: the query, key and value picture and multi-head attention.
  • DeepLearning.AI — Generative AI with LLMs (week 1) — extract: encoder vs decoder and what each is used for.

45 ○ UPCOMING

Adapting a model: prompting, RAG or fine-tuning; LoRA, quantization, RLHF

0 / 170 XP
CUTOFF TARGET
a one-page decision guide for prompting vs RAG vs fine-tuning, and two-sentence answers on LoRA, quantization and RLHF.
01REVIEW

Answer each aloud or on paper before you look anything up. A miss goes into error-log.md with one line of correction.

02CONCEPT

When a model's answers are wrong, you have three levers, tried in this order. Prompting (clear instructions, examples, structure) is cheapest. RAG supplies knowledge the model lacks or that changes often by retrieving documents at question time. Fine-tuning changes behaviour, style or a stable skill; it is a poor way to add facts that change. LoRA fine-tunes small low-rank adapter matrices instead of all the weights (cheap and swappable). Quantization stores weights in fewer bits (8 or 4) to cut memory and speed up serving at some quality cost. RLHF shapes a model toward answers people prefer, using a reward model trained on human comparisons.

03ALTERNATIVES
  • Missing or changing facts → RAG. Auditability or citations → RAG.
  • Wrong format or tone → better prompt and examples first; fine-tune if that fails at scale.
  • Latency or cost at scale → a smaller model, distillation, quantization, caching.
  • A narrow, stable skill with lots of examples → fine-tuning, usually LoRA.
04ROADBLOCK → FIX

Jumping to fine-tuning because it sounds serious. Most failures are prompt or retrieval problems, and you find them by reading failing examples. Fix: build a small eval set first (Day 53), name the failure category, and only then choose a lever.

05KEY IDEAS / HINTS
  • Facts → RAG. Behaviour → prompt, then fine-tune.
  • QLoRA = LoRA on a 4-bit quantized base model, so it fits on one GPU.
  • RLHF in three stages: supervised fine-tune → train a reward model from preference pairs → optimize the policy against it (DPO skips the explicit reward model).
  • Quantization is a serving-cost tool; fine-tuning is a behaviour tool.

ML basics for AI roles: leakage, metrics, overfitting

0 / 170 XP
CUTOFF TARGET
pick the right metric for three scenarios, spot leakage in a given pipeline, and explain how you would detect overfitting.
01REVIEW

Answer each aloud or on paper before you look anything up. A miss goes into error-log.md with one line of correction.

02CONCEPT

You do not need to derive gradient descent, but you must evaluate honestly. Overfitting: the model memorizes training data and fails on new data; detect it as a gap between training and validation scores. Leakage: information from the label or the future sneaks into features or the split (normalizing on the full dataset before splitting, duplicates across train and test, a feature computed after the outcome). Metrics: accuracy misleads on imbalanced data; precision is "of what I flagged, how much was right"; recall is "of what exists, how much I caught"; PR-AUC suits rare positives. For ranking and retrieval you use recall@k, MRR and NDCG (Day 53).

03ALTERNATIVES
  • Favor recall when a miss is expensive (fraud, safety); favor precision when a false alarm is expensive (auto-blocking users).
  • Random split vs time-based split — use a time-based split for anything with a time order.
  • Cross-validation vs a single hold-out — cross-validation for small data, a hold-out for large data.
04ROADBLOCK → FIX

A great metric on a leaky split. 99% accuracy on a 1% positive rate is the "always predict negative" model. Fix: look at class balance first, split by time or by entity, compute a naive baseline, and report precision and recall at a stated threshold.

05KEY IDEAS / HINTS
  • Always compare against a dumb baseline (majority class, last value).
  • Fit scalers, encoders and imputers on the training split only.
  • The threshold is a business decision: choose it from the cost of each kind of error.

0 / 170 XP
CUTOFF TARGET

01REVIEW

Answer each aloud or on paper before you look anything up. A miss goes into error-log.md with one line of correction.

02CONCEPT

Treat an LLM call like any slow, flaky, expensive remote service with a fuzzy contract. A good wrapper has a schema for the output (Pydantic), structured output or function calling so the model returns that shape, validation with one bounded repair attempt, a timeout, retries for transient errors only with backoff and a total budget, logging of prompt version, model, tokens, latency and cost, and versioned prompts stored as files so you can diff and roll back. It reuses Day 8 (Pydantic) and Day 13 (retries).

03ALTERNATIVES
  • Plain text + regex — fragile; avoid.
  • JSON mode — valid JSON, no schema guarantee.
  • Schema-enforced structured output — the provider constrains output to your schema; prefer it, and validate anyway.
  • Function or tool calling — the model picks a function and arguments; the basis of agents (Day 57).
04ROADBLOCK → FIX

Validation failures you did not plan for: prose around the JSON, a missing field, an invented enum value. Fix: schema-enforced output where available, Literal enums with an "unknown" option, one repair retry that feeds the validation error back, then fail loudly into a quarantine. Second wall: unbounded retries burn money. Cap attempts and total time.

05KEY IDEAS / HINTS
  • Use temperature 0 for extraction.
  • Log prompt_version, model, tokens, latency and cost on every call; never log secrets or raw PII.
  • Set a client timeout and an overall request deadline.
  • A prompt is code: file, version, review, test.

Build one tested LLM feature

0 / 170 XP
CUTOFF TARGET
a support-ticket triage function with a 20-case labeled eval set, unit tests on a fake client, and a quality check that fails when accuracy drops.
01REVIEW

Answer each aloud or on paper before you look anything up. A miss goes into error-log.md with one line of correction.

02CONCEPT

An LLM feature needs two kinds of tests, and they must not be mixed. Unit tests use a fake client: fast and deterministic, they cover parsing, retries, validation and routing. Evals call the real model on a labeled set: slower and statistical, they measure quality. The eval is what lets you change a prompt or model and know whether you improved or broke things. This is the smallest version of the discipline you scale up on Days 53–55.

03ALTERNATIVES
  • Unit test vs eval vs online monitoring — unit tests guard your code, evals guard answer quality before release, monitoring guards it after.
  • Exact-match scoring vs LLM-as-judge — use exact match whenever the answer is a label; a judge is for free text (Day 54).
  • Golden set size — 20 cases is a start; grow it from real failures.
04ROADBLOCK → FIX

Flaky tests because a real model runs in CI. Fix: a fake client for unit tests; run the real-model eval separately, at temperature 0, with a threshold that has a tolerance (for example accuracy ≥ 0.85) and results stored per run so you can see drift. Second wall: an eval set the prompt has been tuned to, so the score is inflated. Hold out a few cases you never look at.

05KEY IDEAS / HINTS
  • Write the eval cases before the prompt; include hard and ambiguous ones.
  • Store every eval run (date, prompt version, model, score) in a CSV or JSON file.
  • Keep 5 of the 20 cases as a hidden hold-out.

50 ○ UPCOMING

Embeddings, vector search and hybrid search

0 / 170 XP
CUTOFF TARGET
embed a corpus, store vectors in pgvector, and compare vector-only, keyword-only and hybrid search on the same questions.
01REVIEW

Answer each aloud or on paper before you look anything up. A miss goes into error-log.md with one line of correction.

02CONCEPT

An embedding maps text (or any data) to a vector such that semantically similar things land near each other. Vector search finds nearest neighbours by cosine/dot distance — "retrieve by meaning," not keyword match. Engineers use it for RAG, semantic search, dedup, recommendations, and clustering. This is the foundation of the entire GenAI retrieval stack; under the hood it's "an index for meaning," which maps cleanly onto your index-and-lookup instincts.

03ALTERNATIVES

pgvector (Postgres extension) → you already have Postgres, modest scale, want SQL + vectors together (great default for you). Dedicated vector DBs (Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus) → large scale, advanced filtering, high QPS. FAISS → in-process, max speed, no persistence layer. Managed (Pinecone) → don't want to run infra. Keyword search (BM25) → exact-term matching; often combined with vectors (hybrid).

  • Hybrid search — combine keyword (BM25 or full-text) and vector scores, for example with reciprocal rank fusion. It catches exact terms, names and ids that embeddings blur.
04ROADBLOCK → FIX

The trap: treating cosine similarity as "relevance." High similarity ≠ correct answer — embeddings capture topical closeness, not factual match, so retrieval can return plausible-but-wrong chunks. Fix: hybrid search (BM25 + vector) + reranking (Day 52), and measure with eval (Day 53). Second gotcha: mismatched embedding models between index and query (you must embed queries with the same model you indexed with).

05KEY IDEAS / HINTS

Distance metrics: cosine (most common for text), dot, L2. Dimensionality (e.g. 384, 768, 1536) is fixed by the model. ANN indexes (HNSW, IVFFlat) trade a little recall for big speed — exact search doesn't scale.

06READ

pgvector README — extract: creating a vector column, <=> cosine operator, HNSW/IVFFlat index. Skim a sentence-transformers quickstart — extract: how to embed text locally (free, no API key).

51 ○ UPCOMING

Chunking and ingestion

0 / 170 XP
CUTOFF TARGET
an ingestion pipeline that chunks documents sensibly with metadata, re-runs without duplicates, and a chunk-size choice you can defend.
01REVIEW

Answer each aloud or on paper before you look anything up. A miss goes into error-log.md with one line of correction.

02CONCEPT

Chunking splits documents into retrieval-sized pieces before embedding. It's quietly the highest-leverage knob in RAG quality: too big and a chunk dilutes the relevant bit (poor precision, and you blow the context budget); too small and you lose the surrounding context needed to answer. Engineers spend real effort here because retrieval quality caps the whole system — a perfect LLM can't answer from a bad chunk.

03ALTERNATIVES

Fixed-size + overlap → simplest, decent baseline. Recursive/structural (split on headings/paragraphs) → respects document structure, usually better. Semantic chunking (split on embedding-similarity shifts) → best quality, more compute. Per-document-type (code vs prose vs tables) → when corpus is heterogeneous. Start simple (recursive + overlap), improve if eval says so.

04ROADBLOCK → FIX

The trap: chunking mid-sentence / mid-table so meaning is severed, or zero overlap so an answer spanning a boundary is unretrievable. Fix: overlap (e.g. 10–20%) + structure-aware splitting + attach metadata (source, section, doc id) so you can cite and filter. Second gotcha: not storing enough metadata → you can't filter retrieval (by date/source) or show citations later.

05KEY IDEAS / HINTS

Chunk size + overlap are eval-driven, not guessed. Metadata enables filtered retrieval + citations (which matter for trust). Keep a stable doc-id so re-ingestion is idempotent (the idempotency idea from Day 4: re-embed only changed docs).

52 ○ UPCOMING

The RAG chain: retrieve, rerank, generate with citations

0 / 170 XP
CUTOFF TARGET
an end-to-end function answers from retrieved context with citations, adds a reranking step, and declines a question that is not in the corpus.
01REVIEW

Answer each aloud or on paper before you look anything up. A miss goes into error-log.md with one line of correction.

02CONCEPT

RAG = retrieve relevant chunks, stuff them into the prompt as context, let the LLM generate an answer grounded in them. It exists to fix the LLM's two big failures: stale knowledge and hallucination — ground the model in your retrieved facts. Reranking adds a second, more precise scoring pass over the top-N candidates (a cross-encoder reads query+chunk together) to push the truly relevant chunks to the top before generation. Engineers reach for RAG whenever answers must reflect private/current data.

03ALTERNATIVES

RAG → answers must be grounded in a knowledge base (the default for Q&A over your data). Fine-tuning → when you need behavior/style/format change, not fresh facts (RAG for knowledge, fine-tune for behavior — a key interview distinction). Long-context stuffing → small, fixed corpus that fits in context. Agentic/tool-use (Days 57–58) → when the task needs actions, not just retrieval. Reranking → add when retrieval recall is fine but precision (top-1 quality) is weak.

04ROADBLOCK → FIX

The defining RAG failure: hallucination despite retrieval — the model answers from its own priors and ignores (or contradicts) the context. Fixes: a strict prompt ("answer ONLY from the context; if it's not there, say you don't know"), include citations, and measure faithfulness (Day 53). Second gotcha: retrieving k too high → context bloat, lower-quality chunks dilute the prompt, cost/latency up → rerank and trim.

05KEY IDEAS / HINTS

Pipeline: embed query → ANN retrieve top-N → rerank → take top-k → prompt with context + citations → generate. "Answer only from context, else say I don't know" is the anti-hallucination instruction. Return sources for trust + later eval.

LangChain — RAG tutorial — extract: retriever → prompt → LLM wiring. Skim a cross-encoder reranking explainer — extract: why a second pass beats bi-encoder alone.

53 ○ UPCOMING

Evaluation: Ragas plus retrieval metrics

0 / 170 XP
CUTOFF TARGET
an eval harness scores retrieval (recall@k, MRR, NDCG) and generation (faithfulness, answer relevancy, context precision and recall) over a golden set, giving a baseline you can move.
01REVIEW

Answer each aloud or on paper before you look anything up. A miss goes into error-log.md with one line of correction.

02CONCEPT

A RAG system has two jobs, and you evaluate them separately. Retrieval metrics need labeled relevant documents: recall@k (is a relevant chunk in the top k?), MRR (how high is the first relevant result? average of 1/rank) and NDCG (are the best chunks ranked above the weaker ones, with a rank discount?). Generation metrics, usually from Ragas with an LLM as judge: faithfulness (grounded in the retrieved context, so not hallucinated), answer relevancy (answers the question), context precision and recall. Without a golden set you are tuning by feel.

03ALTERNATIVES

Ragas → RAG-specific, decomposed metrics (the default here). DeepEval / promptfoo → general LLM eval + assertions + CI integration. LLM-as-judge (custom) → when you need a bespoke rubric. Human eval → gold standard, expensive — use to validate your automated metrics. Golden Q&A set → always build one; it's your regression suite.

04ROADBLOCK → FIX

The trap: optimizing one metric and quietly wrecking another — e.g. retrieving more chunks lifts context-recall but tanks faithfulness (more noise → more hallucination). Fix: track the whole vector of metrics, change one variable at a time, and keep a fixed golden set so runs are comparable (regression testing). Second gotcha: LLM-judge noise → use a capable judge model, average over a real question set (not 3 questions), and sanity-check against a few human judgments.

05KEY IDEAS / HINTS
  • Build the golden set first: 25 questions, each with the expected answer and the ids of the chunks that contain it.
  • Retrieval metrics tell you whether retrieval is the problem; faithfulness tells you whether generation is.
  • Change one variable per run and keep the golden set fixed so runs are comparable.

54 ○ UPCOMING

LLM judges, calibration, and debugging a wrong answer stage by stage

0 / 170 XP
CUTOFF TARGET
measure how well your LLM judge agrees with human labels, and walk five wrong answers back to the stage that failed.
01REVIEW

Answer each aloud or on paper before you look anything up. A miss goes into error-log.md with one line of correction.

02CONCEPT

An LLM judge scores answers automatically, but it is a model with its own biases (it likes long answers and its own style) and noise. Calibrate it: label 20–30 answers yourself, compare, and compute agreement; if it disagrees often, change the rubric or the judge model before trusting its numbers. Debugging a wrong answer is a procedure, not a guess. Check the stages in order: was the right document ingested? chunked so the answer survives? retrieved in the top k? kept after reranking? present in the prompt? used by the generation? The first stage that fails is the cause.

03ALTERNATIVES
  • Reference-based scoring (compare with the expected answer) vs reference-free (judge against the context) — reference-based is more reliable when you have the answers.
  • Pairwise comparison (which of two is better) vs absolute scores — pairwise is usually more stable.
  • A stronger judge model vs the same model family — a different, stronger judge reduces self-preference bias.
  • Human review — the ground truth; sample it regularly.
04ROADBLOCK → FIX

Trusting judge scores that nobody checked. Fix: a human-labeled sample, agreement measured (for example Cohen's kappa or simple percent agreement), a written rubric with examples, and re-checking after any judge or prompt change. Second wall: fixing the prompt when retrieval was the failure. Always find the failing stage first.

05KEY IDEAS / HINTS
  • Stage checklist: ingested → chunked → retrieved → reranked → in the prompt → used.
  • Log chunk ids, scores and the final prompt for every request; you cannot debug what you did not record.
  • A judge prompt is code: version it, test it on labeled cases.

  • Eugene Yan — Evaluating the effectiveness of LLM evaluators — extract: known judge biases and how to measure agreement.

AGENTS · LLMOPS · COST

DAY 57–63 / ○ 0/7 / llm-lab

Phase goal: the production half of AI engineering. You build an agent and learn when not to; trace it; protect it against prompt injection and over-permissioned retrieval; budget its cost and tail latency; version and monitor a model in one day; and finish with an incident drill, the exercise interviewers describe as "tell me about a time it broke."

57 ○ UPCOMING

Build a LangGraph agent

0 / 170 XP
CUTOFF TARGET
a LangGraph agent that decides whether to retrieve, query or answer, as an inspectable state graph with a step limit.
01REVIEW

Answer each aloud or on paper before you look anything up. A miss goes into error-log.md with one line of correction.

02CONCEPT

An agent is an LLM that decides and acts in a loop: choose a tool, read the result, decide again, until it can answer. LangGraph models the loop as an explicit state graph (nodes are steps, edges are transitions, state is passed along), which makes the agent inspectable and resumable instead of an opaque while loop. You use an agent when a task needs several steps whose order cannot be known in advance.

03ALTERNATIVES
  • LangGraph — controllable, stateful, inspectable graphs; a good default when you need an agent.
  • A plain tool-use loop — the simplest option and often enough for one or two tool calls.
  • CrewAI or AutoGen — multi-agent framings; reach for them only when one agent measurably fails.
  • No agent — if retrieval or one tool call answers it, skip the agent: agents add latency, cost and failure modes.
04ROADBLOCK → FIX

The classic agent failure: infinite loops / runaway cost — the agent keeps calling tools without converging. Fix: a max-step/recursion limit, a budget cap, and explicit termination conditions in the graph (LangGraph makes these first-class). Second gotcha: the agent confidently calls a tool with wrong/hallucinated args → validate tool inputs (Pydantic), and make tools return structured errors the agent can recover from.

05KEY IDEAS / HINTS
  • Nodes are steps (plan, retrieve, call tool, answer); edges are conditional transitions on state.
  • State carries the conversation and intermediate results; a checkpointer makes a run resumable.
  • Keep tools small, typed and well described.

58 ○ UPCOMING

Agent or workflow? Tool schemas, stop conditions, budgets, MCP

0 / 170 XP
CUTOFF TARGET
a written rule for agent vs fixed workflow, an allow-listed tool registry, hard budgets that stop the agent, and a clear explanation of MCP.
01REVIEW

Answer each aloud or on paper before you look anything up. A miss goes into error-log.md with one line of correction.

02CONCEPT

A workflow fixes the steps in code and uses the model inside individual steps. An agent lets the model choose the steps. Default to the simplest thing that works: one call → a fixed workflow (chain, routing, parallel steps) → an agent only when the path cannot be known ahead of time. A production agent needs typed tool schemas with clear descriptions, an allow-list of tools, stop conditions (final answer, maximum steps, tokens, dollars and wall-clock time), errors returned to the model once and then surfaced, and a trace of every step. MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard for exposing tools and data to LLM apps through servers, so one tool implementation works across many clients.

03ALTERNATIVES
  • Single call — if one prompt solves it, stop here.
  • Fixed workflow — prompt chaining, routing, parallel calls, an evaluator loop: predictable, cheaper, easier to test.
  • Agent loop — only for open-ended tasks.
  • Multi-agent — usually avoid until a single agent has failed on a measured task.
  • Your own thin loop vs a framework — a framework saves time on state and tracing; a thin loop is easier to read.
04ROADBLOCK → FIX

Agents that loop forever, burn money, or call the wrong tool with confident arguments. Fix: hard budgets (steps, tokens, dollars, seconds), tool descriptions with examples and typed arguments, validation on both arguments and results, and an explicit "I cannot do this" exit. Second wall: debugging blind. Trace every step (Day 59).

05KEY IDEAS / HINTS
  • Decision rule: can you draw the steps in advance? Then it is a workflow.
  • Tools are read-only and idempotent by default; put writes behind a confirmation or an approval step.
  • Every tool returns structured results and structured errors.
  • MCP separates tool providers (servers) from LLM apps (clients).

  • Anthropic — Building effective agents — extract: workflow patterns vs agents and when each fits.
  • Model Context Protocol — introduction — extract: what a server, a client and a tool are.

0 / 170 XP
CUTOFF TARGET

01REVIEW

Answer each aloud or on paper before you look anything up. A miss goes into error-log.md with one line of correction.

02CONCEPT

LLM tracing records each step of a generation/agent run — the prompt, retrieved chunks, tool calls, token counts, latency, and cost — so you can debug why an answer was bad and what it cost. Engineers need it because LLM apps fail in opaque ways (bad retrieval? bad prompt? wrong tool?) and cost/latency are real production concerns. This is distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry, Day 14) specialized for LLMs, and it's how you operate the Day 56 RAG service.

03ALTERNATIVES

Langfuse → open-source, self-hostable, great traces + cost + eval hooks (recommended). Arize Phoenix → strong on eval + embedding-drift visualization, open. LangSmith → tight LangChain integration (managed). Plain OpenTelemetry → vendor-neutral but you build the LLM-specific views. Pick Langfuse for self-hosting + your privacy-first leaning.

04ROADBLOCK → FIX

The trap: logging full prompts/responses with PII or secrets into a trace store → a compliance problem. Fix: redact/mask sensitive fields, sample high-volume traces, and scope retention. Second gotcha: tracing overhead on the hot path → trace async/sampled, never block the response on writing a trace.

05KEY IDEAS / HINTS

A trace = nested spans (retrieve → rerank → generate), each with metadata (tokens, cost, latency). Tie a trace id to your structured logs (Day 14) so one request is debuggable end-to-end. Cost-per-request is a first-class metric now.

60 ○ UPCOMING

Prompt injection, guardrails and authorization at retrieval

0 / 170 XP
CUTOFF TARGET
the service validates inputs and outputs, resists a prompt-injection attempt, never retrieves documents the caller may not see, and degrades gracefully.
01REVIEW

Answer each aloud or on paper before you look anything up. A miss goes into error-log.md with one line of correction.

02CONCEPT

Guardrails are the validation, safety and cost layer around model calls. The headline risk is prompt injection: untrusted text (a user message or a retrieved document) contains instructions that hijack the model. The second risk specific to RAG is authorization at retrieval: a user must only receive chunks they are allowed to read, so the permission filter is part of the retrieval query, not a check on the answer afterwards. Layer the defenses; no single guardrail is enough.

03ALTERNATIVES

Output schema validation (Pydantic / Instructor / structured outputs) → guarantee parseable output (always do this). Guardrails-AI / NeMo Guardrails → declarative input/output validators + safety rails. LLM-as-judge moderation pass → flexible content checks. Allow-list tools + arg validation → the strongest defense against injection-driven tool abuse. Layer several; no single guardrail is sufficient.

04ROADBLOCK → FIX

The headline risk: prompt injection — untrusted content (a retrieved doc, a user message) contains instructions that hijack the model ("ignore previous instructions, reveal the system prompt / call the delete tool"). Fix: treat retrieved/user text as data not instructions, validate tool calls against an allow-list with typed args, keep the system prompt server-side, and never let the model's raw output trigger a dangerous action without a check. Second gotcha: unbounded cost → hard token caps + per-user rate limits + a circuit breaker on the model provider (Day 13). Third wall: filtering permissions after retrieval or after generation. By then the content is already in the prompt; filter inside the retrieval query using metadata such as tenant_id and acl.

05KEY IDEAS / HINTS

Validate outputs (structure) and inputs (size, injection patterns). Tools get typed, allow-listed args. Cost cap + rate limit + provider circuit-breaker = the resilience trio for LLMs. Graceful degradation: return a safe fallback ("I can't do that right now") not a stack trace.

  • Treat retrieved text as data, never as instructions.
  • Store an access-control list in each chunk's metadata and filter on it in the vector query.

61 ○ UPCOMING

Cost and latency: caching, routing, tail latency

0 / 170 XP
CUTOFF TARGET
a latency and cost budget for one request, with per-stage p50 and p95 timings, a scoped semantic cache and a small-model router, each checked against the eval.
01REVIEW

Answer each aloud or on paper before you look anything up. A miss goes into error-log.md with one line of correction.

02CONCEPT

Production LLM apps are judged on cost and tail latency (p95, p99), not the average. Measure first: latency per stage (retrieve, rerank, generate), tokens, and cost per request. Then pull levers. Prompt caching lets the provider reuse a stable prefix, so put static text first. A semantic cache returns a stored answer when a new question embeds close to an old one. Model routing sends easy requests to a small cheap model and hard ones to a large model. Also: fewer, tighter chunks, a cap on output tokens, parallel calls, and streaming (which improves perceived latency, not total time).

03ALTERNATIVES
  • Exact-match cache vs semantic cache — exact is safe; semantic has a hit rate but can return a wrong answer.
  • Router by rules vs by a small classifier — rules first; a classifier when rules stop working. Route by measured eval score, not by gut.
  • Bigger model vs better retrieval — often better retrieval is cheaper than a bigger model.
  • API vs self-hosted — self-hosting trades per-token cost for operations work.
04ROADBLOCK → FIX

A semantic cache that returns a wrong answer, or another user's answer. Fix: a high similarity threshold, a cache key scoped by tenant, permissions and document version, a TTL, invalidation when the index changes, and measured hit quality. Second wall: optimizing the average while p99 times out. Fix: per-stage timeouts, parallel retrieval, and a fallback path.

05KEY IDEAS / HINTS
  • p95 is the time that 95% of requests beat; the slowest 5% are what users complain about.
  • Track cache hit rate and false-hit rate. Both are metrics.
  • A cost budget has a number: cost per request × requests per day.

62 ○ UPCOMING

Model registry and drift in one day

0 / 170 XP
CUTOFF TARGET
a small classifier registered in MLflow with a production alias, served at /predict, with an Evidently drift report that produces a number you could alert on.
01REVIEW

Answer each aloud or on paper before you look anything up. A miss goes into error-log.md with one line of correction.

02CONCEPT

ML platform questions come in four parts: how do you version a model, promote it, roll it back, and know when the data has changed. A model registry stores versions with metadata and aliases (such as production), so serving loads "the production model" and a rollback is moving an alias. Drift means the input data (data drift) or the link between inputs and the label (concept drift) changed, so a once-good model degrades. You detect it by comparing recent data with a reference window, alert on a drift score, and write down the rule that triggers a retrain.

03ALTERNATIVES
  • MLflow registry vs a cloud registry (SageMaker, Azure ML, Vertex, Unity Catalog) — same ideas; pick what your platform already runs.
  • Evidently vs hand-written tests (PSI, KS test) — a library saves time; know the underlying statistic.
  • Retrain on a schedule vs on drift — a schedule is simple; drift-triggered retrains need a trustworthy signal.
04ROADBLOCK → FIX

Alerting on every small drift and teaching everyone to ignore the alert. Fix: pick a few important features, set thresholds from a baseline window, and alert on a sustained shift. Second wall: drift in inputs is not proof the model is worse; if labels arrive later, track real performance too.

05KEY IDEAS / HINTS
  • A model signature (input schema) enforces the contract at serve time.
  • Rollback = move the alias back; never delete versions you may need.
  • Data drift is detectable without labels; performance drift usually needs labels.

  • MLflow — Model Registry — extract: register, aliases, load by alias.
  • Evidently docs — extract: reference vs current dataset, a data drift report, extracting a numeric drift score.

Architecture and scaffold the slice

0 / 170 XP
CUTOFF TARGET

01REVIEW

Answer each aloud or on paper before you look anything up. A miss goes into error-log.md with one line of correction.

02CONCEPT

A capstone fails when it is a pile of notebooks. Start with the boxes: CDC feed → Spark Streaming → Iceberg raw → dbt staging and marts with a quality gate → serving (/ask) → Prometheus and Grafana, with reconciliation and the agent hanging off the side. Every box gets one owner file and one health check on day one, so integration is never the surprise at the end.

03ALTERNATIVES
  • Everything in one compose file vs several — one file for a portfolio project; it must start with one command.
